ready.description: A sharp countertrend bear spike of several consecutive bear trend bars reaches the moving average from above and the current bar closes up: buy near its close.
ready.pseudocode: consecutiveBearTrendBars(bodyFraction) >= spikeBars && low[0] <= ema(close, emaLength)[0] + supportAtr * atr(atrLookback) && close[0] > open[0]

complexity.reason: needs an EMA plus a consecutive-trend-bar run; the book's 'established bull trend' qualifier is dropped as research-grade

catalog_match.note: the catalog rule is a plain close-vs-average test; this is a spike run terminating at the average from the far side, so different bars

ready.merge_notes: The book's example is a news-driven overnight gap in an uptrend; the mechanical form keeps the spike-into-support structure and drops the news cause. The always-in qualifier is dropped rather than inherited, which is why this is B and not C -- the remaining terms all have bar-level definitions.

ready.description: After an extended quiet period, an unusually large trend bar breaking out of the tight range should not be entered directly -- require a confirming pullback first.
ready.pseudocode: countif(k in 1..lookback, (high[k] - low[k]) <= smallRangeFraction * atr(atrLookback)) >= minQuietBars && (high[0] - low[0]) >= breakoutBarMultiple * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: a rolling quiet-bar count plus a size-relative-to-ATR test on the current bar; no cross-bar state

catalog_match.note: the catalog rule is only the outsized-bar half; this adds the preceding quiet run and reads as a block rather than a trigger

ready.merge_notes: The book says 30 to 60 minutes of quiet; minQuietBars is that in bars and needs the timeframe fixed at authoring. Written as a block on the immediate entry, so it pairs with BreakoutPullbackEntry as the permitted alternative.

ready.description: The opening range is already a large fraction of the recent average daily range, so a later breakout is unlikely to become a strong trend: down-weight or block breakout entries for the session.
ready.pseudocode: openingRangeSet && (openingRangeHigh - openingRangeLow) > weakBreakoutFraction * avgDailyRange(dayLookback)

complexity.reason: needs the session's opening range and a multi-session average range, then one comparison

ready.merge_notes: The mirror of the small-opening-range breakout-mode filters mined into other buckets; recorded here because it gates breakout entries specifically.

ready.description: The session gapped beyond the prior session's extreme and the first bar of the session is a reversal bar: enter when the next bar closes back through that first bar's far side -- a failed breakout of the gap.
ready.pseudocode: barsIntoSession == 1 && open[1] < prevSessionLow && close[1] > open[1] && (close[1] - open[1]) >= bodyFraction * (high[1] - low[1]) && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: session-boundary state plus the prior session's extreme; the bar tests are fixed offsets

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from FailedBreakoutOfPriorSessionExtreme: that one fires on any bar of the session that pierces and recovers the level, this one only on the session's very first bar and requires a reversal bar plus a confirming close.

ready.description: When the market gaps open beyond the prior day's range, do not chase the open: wait for an early pullback that retraces partway back into the gap, then enter once that pullback fails and price resumes away from the prior day's range.
ready.pseudocode: open[0] > prevSessionHigh && lowest(low, barsIntoSession) <= open[0] - gapFillFraction * (open[0] - prevSessionHigh) && close[0] > open[0] && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: the prior day's extreme, a gap detector, an intraday retracement measurement and a reversal-bar test chained together

ready.merge_notes: The book gates this on a daily buy/sell setup being in force; that higher-timeframe flag is dropped rather than inherited (the engine is single-timeframe), which keeps the rule at B. gapFillFraction is invented -- the book gives no depth for how far into the gap the pullback must travel.

ready.description: The session has already broken beyond one side of the day's range by only a small amount and has now reversed to break beyond the other side by a small amount: fade the second break, expecting a quiet range rather than a trend.
ready.pseudocode: shallowBreakoutOccurred(sessionHigh, maxExtension) && low[0] < sessionLow && (sessionLow - low[0]) <= maxExtension * sessionRange && close[0] > open[0]

complexity.reason: tracks shallow breakouts on both sides within the session plus a size test on each extension

ready.merge_notes: A two-sided cousin of TwiceFailedBreakoutAttempt (which counts repeated failures on ONE side); kept separate because the second break is on the opposite side, so they never fire on the same bar.

ready.description: After a strong multi-session trend leg, price has stayed inside that leg's range without retracing past a fraction of it for up to K sessions; a breakout beyond the pause range in the leg's original direction is a high-conviction trend-resumption entry.
ready.pseudocode: priorLegDirection == 1 && sessionsSincePriorLeg <= maxPauseSessions && retracementSincePriorLeg <= maxRetraceFraction * priorLegHeight && close[0] > pauseRangeHigh

complexity.reason: cross-session state remembering a leg's direction, height and the pause range it settled into, over many sessions

ready.merge_notes: The pause need not be a single tight box the whole time, which is why the state is a retracement cap rather than a range detector -- that keeps it out of the trading-range design decision.

ready.description: In a one-sided trend, the FIRST against-trend trend bar in a long while printed within the last few bars, and this bar has now closed above that bar's high (long) — the first bear spike in a strong bull trend is almost always just a bull flag.
ready.pseudocode: k = smallest index in 1..flagBars with (close[k] < open[k] && (open[k]-close[k]) >= bodyFraction*(high[k]-low[k])); k exists && countif(j in k+1..k+strongBars: bear trend bar[j]) == 0 && close[0] > high[k]

complexity.reason: a backward scan for the FIRST qualifying bar, whose index k then drives both a second count window and the price comparison — a variable offset, not a fixed lag

ready.merge_notes: Kept whole rather than split: the 'no other opposite trend bar in the preceding 20 bars' term is StrongTrendBarCount negated, but it must be measured FROM the found bar k, not from bar 0, so it cannot be a separate pane. Everything is bounded and deterministic (scan at most flagBars bars back), so the definition is clear — B, not C. Brooks states it only for the FIRST opposite spike, which is why the zero-count window is part of the rule.

ready.description: Exit at the first or second bar after entry if that bar did not close as a strong with-trend trend bar — Brooks's 'strong closes mean swing it, weak closes mean scalp it', recast as a binary scalp-versus-hold exit.
ready.pseudocode: n = ctx.BarsSinceEntry(); n <= maxBars && barWeak(n) && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() > 0   // barWeak(k) = close[k] <= open[k] || (close[k]-open[k]) < strongBodyFraction * (high[k]-low[k]), direction-adjusted

complexity.reason: must index the bar series by BarsSinceEntry and adjust the body test by the open position's direction

catalog_match.note: NumBarsIfProfitable exits on elapsed bars plus a profit sign. This adds the bar-strength test on the entry bar itself and only fires in the first maxBars+1 bars, so it is an early-scalp exit rather than a time stop.

ready.merge_notes: The chapter's only bar-level idea; the rest is intrabar behaviour in the final seconds of a bar, which is below the data. The miner recorded that Brooks's actual point is about position SIZE, which the engine cannot express — this is the honest binary approximation and should be labelled as such when authored. B because the BarsSinceEntry indexing plus the direction-dependent body test is real machinery, but the definition itself is unambiguous.

ready.description: The first bar of a session opens beyond the prior session's extreme — above the prior session's high (long) / below its low (short).
ready.pseudocode: isFirstBarOfSession(0) && open[0] > priorSessionHigh

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and the prior session's high/low carried as state

ready.merge_notes: All three quote the same glossary line from different volumes. Brooks allows either the prior session's last bar or the whole prior day as reference; the whole-session high/low won, equally cheap once the accumulator exists and the stronger reading.

ready.description: The session's first bar opens at least K x ATR above the prior session's close (long) / below it (short) — a signed gap-size test, the gap read as a spike in its own direction.
ready.pseudocode: isFirstBarOfSession(0) && open[0] - priorSessionClose >= gapAtrMultiple * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: session boundary plus the prior session's close and an ATR

ready.merge_notes: T21-49 treats the gap as the spike of a spike-and-channel day, T23-05 as a directional tilt; behaviourally one signed test. T23-05 uses 0.5 ATR, T21-49 1.0 — both recorded, 1.0 the default. Kept apart from the unsigned SessionGapAtrMagnitude.

ready.description: The session's first bar opens at least K x ATR away from the prior session's close in either direction — a large-gap day flag, identical on both sides.
ready.pseudocode: isFirstBarOfSession(0) && fabs(open[0] - priorSessionClose) >= gapAtrMultiple * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: session boundary plus the prior session's close and an ATR

ready.merge_notes: Same measurement as SessionGapAtrDirectional but unsigned, so it passes both sides after a gap either way — Brooks's 'large gaps lead to trend days in either direction'. T19-14's absolute 8-point Emini threshold lost to T12-03's ATR multiple, which is instrument-independent.

ready.description: Over the last N bars the lowest low has stayed above the prior session's close (long) / the highest high below it (short) — the opening gap has not been filled early.
ready.pseudocode: lowest(low, checkBars) > priorSessionClose

complexity.reason: window extreme against the prior session's close carried as state

ready.merge_notes: T19-15 only, carried as the atomic half of its composite with T19-14 — the gap-size half is SessionGapAtrMagnitude. Brooks: large gaps that do not reverse early usually start a strong trend day. checkBars 12 is the miner's reading of 'early'.

ready.description: Early in the session, price closes beyond the high of the session's first bar (long) / below its low (short) — a trend-from-the-open breakout.
ready.pseudocode: barsIntoSession(0) >= 1 && barsIntoSession(0) <= maxBarsIntoSession && close[0] > sessionFirstBarHigh

complexity.reason: session-relative bar index plus the session's first bar high/low carried as state

ready.merge_notes: T23-13's gap term is SessionGapAtrMagnitude and its strong-trend-bar term belongs to bar_anatomy; carried here is the atomic remainder. The book itself says the trade is good even without a gap (p419), so no gap term is bundled in.

ready.description: A climax bar that arrives after the always-in direction has held the same way for at least minRunBars bars -- the exhaustion form, where the biggest-looking breakout of the move is the one most likely to fail.
ready.pseudocode: ClimaxBar[0] && alwaysInRunLength(0) >= minRunBars, where alwaysInRunLength counts the bars since AlwaysInDirection last flipped

complexity.reason: needs the always-in flip persisted as a bar counter on top of the climax bar test

catalog_match.note: as ClimaxBar, plus the run gate

ready.merge_notes: Held apart from ClimaxBar rather than dropped as a composition, because the run gate has no independent rule to AND against: the always-in run LENGTH is not itself a mined candidate anywhere in this bucket, and the whole point of both sources is that the same bar means the opposite thing early and late in a trend. Measured against the decided AlwaysInDirection (two consecutive strong trend bars, body >= 0.6, tails <= 0.2) rather than a bars-since-swing-pivot count -- the alternative is recorded in design_decisions. Book run lengths: 10 or 20 bars (V24-20), 10 bars (T06-25), 30 (T02-10), 40 (V04-08); default 10, the value both sources here give. T06-25 supplies the softer 1.5 x ATR over 10 bars, used as the default here since the run gate is already doing selection work.

ready.description: At least minSpikes separate same-direction spikes -- runs of at least spikeBars consecutive strong trend bars, each run separated from the next by a non-spike bar -- within the last windowBars. Brooks: every spike, one bar or many, is a climax.
ready.pseudocode: count of disjoint runs of >= spikeBars consecutive StrongTrendBar(up) bars inside bars 0..windowBars-1 >= minSpikes

complexity.reason: run detection with state over a window, on top of the shared spike primitive

catalog_match.note: that rule needs one run of N bars each closing above the close N bars ago; this needs several separated runs of strong trend BODIES, so the bars differ

ready.merge_notes: The run form of the climax-classification decision, built on the already-decided spike primitive (StrongTrendBarRun / StrongTrendBarCount) rather than redefining it. T15-57 is the cleanest statement (disjoint runs of >= 2 bull trend bars, 3 within 30 bars) and supplies the defaults; T10-16 (stray, absorbed) is the same test on bear spikes with an added reversal-bar entry term, which is left to bar_anatomy. VP1-20 and V01-16 count 'climaxes without much of a pullback' since the session start -- the same idea with an intraday anchor and the pullback qualifier; both are folded in and the pullback qualifier is left to the decided tight-channel measure in its own pane. Threshold 3 here (all four sources say three) against 2 on ConsecutiveClimaxBarCount, which is the book's own asymmetry: two big bars is a double top, three spikes is a wedge.

ready.description: A spike in one direction immediately followed by a spike in the opposite direction: the climactic reversal. Brooks's expectation is a transition into a trading range whose eventual breakout runs about the height of the first spike.
ready.pseudocode: strongTrendBarRun(down, spikeBars) ending at bar 0 && strongTrendBarRun(up, spikeBars) ending at bar spikeBars + gapBars or closer

complexity.reason: two opposite-direction runs located relative to each other, on the shared spike primitive

ready.merge_notes: The one candidate in this bucket for the chapter title's own pattern ('a spike followed by a spike in the opposite direction'), and the only climax rule that is a two-sided shape rather than a count or a size. Built on the decided spike primitive. The measured-move consequence Brooks attaches to it (the breakout runs the height of the first spike) is a target, not a condition, and is left to the exits/targets pass.

ready.description: A run of at least runBars consecutive same-direction strong trend bars ended on the previous bar: this bar is not one (a small bar, a tailed bar, an inside bar, a doji or an opposite bar broke the streak). Brooks: the climax ends as soon as the strong trending behaviour is interrupted.
ready.pseudocode: strongTrendBarRun(up, runBars) ending at bar 1 && !StrongTrendBar(up)[0]

complexity.reason: a consecutive-run counter on the shared strong-trend-bar test, plus the break condition

catalog_match.note: the mining file guessed that rule; it counts closes above the close N bars ago, not strong trend BODIES, and has no 'and the streak just broke' term

ready.merge_notes: The event that Brooks uses to time a fade -- not the climax itself but the bar that ends it -- so it is behaviourally distinct from every count rule here and from the spike primitive it is built on. Three bars is the book's example; runBars is the input.

ready.description: Exit the open position once a second same-direction climax has printed -- take profits into the climax, or on the first opposite-body bar after it.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ConsecutiveClimaxBarCount(minClimaxes = 2) && (exitOnClimaxClose || close[0] < open[0])

complexity.reason: the climax count plus position state

catalog_match.note: same shape -- an exit on a run of with-trend bars -- but keyed on climax bars rather than on N consecutive rising closes

ready.merge_notes: Cannot be composed from ConsecutiveClimaxBarCount: that is an Entry, exits are ORed and an Entry cannot sit in the exit pane, so the exit form has to exist separately -- the same reason the catalog carries ConsecutiveCloseExit alongside MomentumConsecutiveBars. The exitOnClimaxClose toggle picks between selling into the climax bar's close and waiting for the first opposite-body bar; both are in the quote.

ready.description: The session's move from the open has reached rangeFraction of the recent average daily range, so further movement in that direction is treated as exhausted and countertrend setups are favoured.
ready.pseudocode: sessionRange(k) = the high-low of session k built from the intraday bars; abs(close[0] - sessionOpen) >= rangeFraction * average(sessionRange, dailyLookback)

complexity.reason: per-session high/low accumulated on the intraday series and averaged over the last N sessions, plus a session-open reference

ready.merge_notes: Kept because it is the one exhaustion measure in the bucket that is scaled to the DAY rather than to the bar, and it needs no climax primitive at all. The mined candidate assumed a second daily data stream; rewritten to accumulate session ranges on the intraday series, which is what makes it hard rather than out of scope. Intraday-only, tagged per the standing convention.

ready.description: The exception clause on the with-trend gate: a countertrend entry is permitted only if, within the last N bars, price has already closed beyond the trend line drawn through the last two same-side swing pivots, OR a trend-channel-line overshoot has reversed. Until one of those has happened, no countertrend entry is allowed however good the setup looks.
ready.pseudocode:
trendLine = line through the last two swing lows (strength pivotStrength);
barsSince(close[i] < trendLine[i]) <= lookback || barsSince(trendChannelLineOvershootReversal) <= lookback

complexity.reason: needs swing pivots, a two-point line projection forward, and a bars-since counter on each of the two conditions

catalog_match.note: no line-projection rule exists in the corpus

ready.merge_notes: V02-35's own note calls it 'the single most repeated rule of the trilogy', and this bucket bears that out. V02-35 is the cleanest statement and wins. R26-02 adds a steepness precondition ('if the trend is STEEP, never trade countertrend unless...') — the steepness measure is dropped as unstated and the rule is taken at its stronger reading, applying whenever the with-trend gate is on. V07-15 restates it as 'exceptionally strong momentum, no shorts until the bears show a significant sign of strength' and its own mining note flags it as a likely duplicate of V02-35; agreed. R10-01 adds 'at a magnet level' and an alternative escape ('or the move is a pullback in a higher time frame trend'); the magnet gate belongs to support_resistance_levels and the higher-time-frame escape needs a second data series, so both are dropped and only the shared permission clause is merged. Kept SEPARATE from AlwaysInBlockCountertrend: that filter blocks countertrend entries outright, this one re-opens them on a specific event, and they will not fire on the same bars.

ready.description: The day is a trend day and its direction is up (long side): once at least `openingBars` bars of the session have printed, the close sits at least `trendDayAtr` x ATR above the session's open. While that holds, only with-trend entries are permitted for the rest of the session.
ready.pseudocode: barsIntoSession >= openingBars && (close[0] - sessionOpen) >= trendDayAtr * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: session-open detection and a bars-into-session counter, both reset on the date change, plus an ATR

catalog_match.note: the corpus has no session-scoped rule; CalendarBoundaryExit reads Date but not the session open

ready.merge_notes: TP4-07 is the stray sent over from ema_relations and it is the cleanest of the three: 'sign of close minus session open once the opening range has printed'. It wins over R08-24's alternative ('a fraction of the session's bars closed on one side of the EMA'), which is recorded as the second option, and over TP4-08, which adds no test of its own — it is TP4-07 used as a with-trend gate. Deliberately kept separate from AlwaysInDirection: this resets every session and reads the session open, where always-in is continuous across the whole series, and the two will disagree on any gap day.

ready.description: The session opened with a strong trend leg and has since spent several hours inside a tight range: favour continuation in the morning leg's direction and block fresh countertrend entries. The tighter that midday range against the average daily range, the stronger the read.
ready.pseudocode: morningLegDirection != 0 && barsSinceMorningLeg >= minMiddayBars && (middayRangeHigh - middayRangeLow) <= tightRangeFraction * avgDailyRange

complexity.reason: a session-scoped morning-leg direction, a running midday range measured from the end of that leg, and an average daily range over completed sessions

ready.merge_notes: T01-07 previews the pattern in one sentence ('strong trend on the open, then a tight trading range for several hours, good chance of a trend resumption day') and T25-03 is the fleshed-out chapter version with the tight-range fraction; same rule, T25-03's numbers win. T25-03's page 454 caveat — the midday action can be a weakly trending countertrend drift rather than a flat range — is NOT mechanized; tightRangeFraction is the proxy for both forms and should be loosened rather than special-cased. Depends on SessionTrendDayDirection for the morning leg.

ready.description: The correction has now lasted at least F times as many BARS as the trend leg it is correcting — Brooks's duration rule of thumb, used to hold off a continuation entry until the correction has had time to finish. Identical both sides: it counts bars, not direction.
ready.pseudocode: barsSinceCorrectionStart >= correctionFraction * trendLegLengthInBars

complexity.reason: needs a swing detector to bound the prior leg in bars, plus a persistent counter for the correction; the comparison itself is trivial once those exist

ready.merge_notes: Duration, where DeepPullbackRetracement is depth — both listed on each other so the authoring pass sees the pair and can test whether they coincide. 'About half' is Brooks's phrasing; 0.5 is a reading, and the source's example was a 20 to 30 bar bear channel.

ready.description: The session so far is a trading-range day: the range travelled since the open (highest high minus lowest low of the session's bars) is no more than F of the recent average daily range. Identical both sides. Used to permit fade and scalp entries and to suppress with-trend swing entries.
ready.pseudocode: sessionHigh = highest(high, barsSinceSessionOpen)[0]; sessionLow = lowest(low, barsSinceSessionOpen)[0]; (sessionHigh - sessionLow) <= dayRangeFraction * average(priorDailyRange, adrLookbackDays)

complexity.reason: needs a session boundary (running high/low reset on each new date) and a rolling average of completed daily ranges

catalog_match.note: Nothing in the catalog is session-scoped except TimeOfDayExit and TimeWindow, which only read the clock.

ready.merge_notes: The day-scale sibling of RangeWidthBelowAtrMultiple, kept apart because its window is the session rather than a bar count and it therefore needs the session machinery. The width definition is chosen for the same reason it won at bar scale, and it beats the two counting definitions in the sources: T07-33 wants K reversals plus tailed bars in the first N bars and R21-14 wants four or five reversals in the first hour, both of which need a 'reversal' defined before they can be coded and both of which are only predictive of the day type, not a measurement of it. T17-04 states the gate as plain NOT(trend day); T05-12 uses the classification permissively (a trending trading range day often reverses late). minSessionBars guards the classification from firing on the first few bars, when every session is narrow. dayRangeFraction is a fresh reading, not a book number -- Brooks never quantifies a trading-range day.

ready.description: The close sits in the bottom fraction of the day's range so far (long) / the top fraction (short) -- the session-scoped form of the range-position test, which is how Brooks states it for trading-range days. Mirrored.
ready.pseudocode: dayHigh = highest(high, barsSinceSessionOpen)[0]; dayLow = lowest(low, barsSinceSessionOpen)[0]; (close[0] - dayLow) <= nearExtremeFraction * (dayHigh - dayLow)

complexity.reason: a running session high and low reset on each new date, then one ratio

ready.merge_notes: Kept separate from RangeExtremeFade because the window is the session, not a bar count -- the two disagree constantly (early in a session the day's range is a handful of bars, late it may be wider than any 20-bar window). V25-01 states it as a block ('do not buy near the top of the day's range'), RP4-21 as a permission (look for a reversal at the day's extreme going into the last hour or two); one is the other flipped, so they are one rule. RP4-21's final-hours term is the catalog's TimeWindow AND-ed alongside, not carried here. V25-01's day-type gate is TradingRangeDay, likewise a separate pane.

ready.description: This bar's high-low range is at least as large as the average bar range of the session so far. Identical both sides. Brooks's gate on range scalps: a tight range is only worth fading when the bars in it are big enough to pay.
ready.pseudocode: sessionAvgBarRange = average(high - low, barsSinceSessionOpen); (high[0] - low[0]) >= sizeMultiple * sessionAvgBarRange

complexity.reason: a running session sum of bar ranges and a bar count, both reset on each new date

catalog_match.note: BarRangeAboveStd compares the bar against a fixed N-bar mean plus K standard deviations; this compares it against the session-to-date mean, whose window grows through the day. Also near bar_anatomy_trend_doji's merged BarRangeAboveAtrMultiple.

ready.merge_notes: The session-average bar range is the same measure R21-13 uses for a money stop (exits_stops bucket) -- one shared primitive, flagged for the roll-up. R22-14's other half, Brooks allowing a four- or five-point range to still count as tight when the bars are large, is the reason RangeWidthBelowAtrMultiple divides by ATR rather than by points: a wide-bar tight range already scores as tight on the ATR scale, so that half needs no rule.

ready.description: The current pullback has retraced at least fraction F of the prior leg -- once pullbacks get this deep, Brooks says they behave like trading ranges rather than flags, and a new high above the old one is a range breakout likely to fail. Mirrored.
ready.pseudocode: legHigh = highest(high, legLookback)[0]; pullbackLow = lowest(low, pullbackLookback)[0]; legLow = lowest(low, legLookback)[0]; (legHigh - pullbackLow) >= maxPullbackFraction * (legHigh - legLow)

complexity.reason: three window extremes; the book's swing-pivot anchoring is replaced by nested windows

ready.merge_notes: TP3-35 anchors the leg on swing pivots (lastSwingHigh, priorSwingLow, pivotStrength 2). Replaced by nested highest/lowest windows per the most-mechanizable rule -- no pivot search, no persistent pivot state, and the corpus already reaches for Highest/Lowest everywhere. swing_structure has merged a related PullbackDepthFromRecentHigh; the roll-up should compare the two and keep one. Brooks's page-314 aside is worth carrying to the authoring pass: every trading range sits inside either a bull or a bear trend, so this rule is a trend-quality filter, not a regime flag on its own.

ready.description: At least K of the last N completed DAILY bars closed as strong bull trend days — a large bull body relative to the day's range. A higher-time-frame confirmation for entries on the trading timeframe. Mirrored for bear days.
ready.pseudocode: countIf(d, 0, dayLookback-1, dailyClose[d] > dailyOpen[d] && (dailyClose[d]-dailyOpen[d]) >= strongBodyFraction*(dailyHigh[d]-dailyLow[d])) >= minStrongDays

complexity.reason: needs daily bars — either a second data series or session aggregation carried across the date change — which nothing in the corpus currently does

catalog_match.note: no corpus rule reads a second timeframe

ready.merge_notes: Both volumes print the identical sentence ('the market has had several strong bull trend days recently'). R02-12 leaves 'trend day' to a design decision and reaches for the session-level classification; T00-47 gives a concrete daily-bar body test, which wins because it needs no session state at all when the strategy already runs on M1440 bars — on a daily chart this degenerates to StrongTrendBarCount and should be authored as that rather than duplicated. Defaults from T00-47 (5 days, 2 strong); R02-12's were 10 and 2.

ready.description: Since the current trend leg began, the DEEPEST pullback so far has stayed below a threshold — expressed as a fraction of the average daily range (portable) or as a fixed number of points (Brooks's own form). This is the small-pullback trend, the strongest kind of trend there is. The rule tracks a running extreme and the maximum give-back from it.

complexity.reason: a running extreme, a give-back tracker, an average daily range over completed sessions, and a reset rule for when the leg starts

catalog_match.note: ProfitProtector tracks give-back from peak PROFIT on an open position; this tracks give-back from peak PRICE with no position involved. Structurally similar, behaviourally unrelated

ready.merge_notes: Three statements of one measurement. T23-06 is the state primitive (track the largest pullback since the trend began), T23-07 is the test against a fraction of the average daily range, and V00-40 is the same test with Brooks's raw Emini number (pullbacks under 3 to 4 points on a 12-point average range — which IS about 0.25 of the range, so the two forms agree). Merged rather than kept apart because a state primitive with no comparison is not a rule and the comparison is meaningless without the state. The fraction form is the default and the points form is kept as a second input for exact reproduction of the book's example. T23-07's session scoping (trend-from-open flag, T23-03) is NOT baked in: reset-on-leg-start is the general form and the session reset is one choice of leg.

ready.description: The pullback now underway is at least `growthMultiple` times as deep as the largest pullback seen earlier in this trend. On a small-pullback trend day Brooks expects exactly this later in the session and warns against reading it as a reversal — so the rule is most useful NEGATED, as 'this pullback is still within the trend's normal size'.
ready.pseudocode:
currentPullbackDepth = runningHigh - low[0];
currentPullbackDepth >= growthMultiple * pullbackMaxBefore

complexity.reason: needs both the running pullback depth and the prior maximum held apart from each other

ready.merge_notes: Brooks gives 'about twice the size' and 'two-thirds of these days'; growthMultiple defaults to 1.5 as the conservative reading, 2.0 recorded. The 11:00 a.m. gate is CATALOG's TimeWindow in a separate pane, not part of this rule. Kept separate from MaxPullbackDepthBelowThreshold: that one caps the historical maximum, this one compares the live pullback to it, and they fire on different bars.

ready.description: In a strong trend, buy a dip of a fixed size rather than a pattern: enter when price trades a set fraction of the trend's AVERAGE prior pullback below the running high. Sized to the trend's own behaviour, so it adapts as the trend's pullbacks grow.
ready.pseudocode:
avgPullback = mean of the completed pullback depths since the trend began;
low[0] <= runningHigh - avgPullbackFraction * avgPullback

complexity.reason: needs every completed pullback depth of the current trend accumulated and averaged, not just the maximum

ready.merge_notes: Shares MaxPullbackDepthBelowThreshold's give-back tracker but needs a running SUM and COUNT of completed pullbacks rather than a maximum, so it is a genuine extension of that state rather than a use of it. Brooks says 'equal to or slightly less than the average prior pullbacks', hence the 0.9 default. Under the standing convention the resting limit becomes signal-bar close then next-bar open.

ready.description: Past the first hour of the session, the close has broken beyond the opening range by at least `breakMultiple` times that range's own height — treat the day as a trend day and take only with-trend entries for the rest of it.
ready.pseudocode: barsIntoSession >= firstHourBars && close[0] > openingRangeHigh + breakMultiple * (openingRangeHigh - openingRangeLow)

complexity.reason: session-open detection, a bars-into-session counter and a latched opening range, all reset on the date change

ready.merge_notes: The candidate's own note is honest that Brooks's trend-day test is pattern recognition and the opening-range break is a proxy. Kept apart from the context_regime_always_in bucket's SessionTrendDayDirection, which measures from the session OPEN against an ATR; this measures from the opening RANGE against its own height, and on a wide-range opening they disagree. The two should be tested against each other before either is trusted.

ready.description: A new extreme has been made and, since the first leg completed, no bar has closed back through even a shallow retracement of that leg — the ABSENCE of any proper pullback, read as a sign of strength in its own right.

complexity.reason: needs the first leg's start and extreme remembered, plus a latch that clears on the first qualifying retracement

ready.merge_notes: Needs leg START and leg HEIGHT in price, which the settled leg definition (HighLowBarCount, R17-01, leg_counting) does not provide — that counter gives leg numbers, not prices — so this needs swing pivots regardless and is graded accordingly. Related to HigherLowStreak and MaxPullbackDepthBelowThreshold, which measure 'no pullback' by bars and by depth respectively; all three should be compared before more than one is authored.

ready.description: Price has gone at least N consecutive bars without any bar touching the N-bar EMA -- Brooks's '20 gap bars', a strong but overdone trend.
ready.pseudocode: barsSinceEmaTouch = (low[0] <= ema(close, emaLength)[0] && high[0] >= ema(close, emaLength)[0]) ? 0 : barsSinceEmaTouch[1] + 1; barsSinceEmaTouch >= gapBarsRequired

complexity.reason: an EMA plus one persistent bars-since-touch counter; no window loop

catalog_match.note: Nothing in the catalog carries a bars-since-event counter; MomentumConsecutiveBars is the closest shape but counts a price relation over a fixed window, not a reset-on-event streak.

ready.merge_notes: R13-01's definition wins: one persistent counter that resets when the bar's range straddles the EMA, tested against a threshold. The four 'twenty gap bars' restatements (R00-24, V00-14, T00-13, T19-13) all express it as a fixed-length loop over the EmaGapBar primitive, which costs a 20-deep loop and an EMA read per bar for the same bars; kept as citations. Direction is dropped with the loop: the counter is direction-agnostic (sides 'same'), which differs from the mirrored loop forms only when price gaps clean across the EMA without a straddling bar -- rare, and recorded here as the cost of the cheaper machine. Book thresholds: 20 (five sources, the default), 30 (V23-01), 45 on the daily (TP1-09). V23-01 also fades the extreme streak countertrend and predicts an EMA touch within 10 bars; the fade is this same rule with the placement flipped, and the 10-bar window is a target/exit idea not carried here. Brooks says outright that 20 'is arbitrary ... any large number of bars', so gapBarsRequired is an optimizer input, not a book constant. Kept apart from the one-bar EmaGapBar per MERGE.md.

ready.description: The first bar to touch the EMA after a run of N bars that never touched it, closing back on the trend side: the '20 gap bar' pullback buy.
ready.pseudocode: barsSinceEmaTouch[1] >= gapBarsRequired && low[0] <= ema(close, emaLength)[0] && close[0] > ema(close, emaLength)[0]

complexity.reason: the bars-since-touch counter read one bar back, plus a straddle test

ready.merge_notes: Carried whole even though it looks like EmaGapBarRun AND EmaTouch, because it is NOT that conjunction: the counter resets to 0 on the touch bar itself, so EmaGapBarRun evaluates FALSE on exactly the bar this rule fires. The rule needs the counter's PREVIOUS value, which no pair of ANDed panes can express. R26-12 states it as 'the first pullback that touches the moving average in more than 20 bars', T18-18 as a limit order one tick above the average once 20 bars have passed without a touch, T17-08 as the '20 gap bar pullback setup'; identical bars, and the limit-order mechanics collapse under the standing signal-bar-close/next-bar-open convention. Brooks's 'buyers at the moving average' claim is what the entry monetizes; the touch tolerance in the sources (0 to 1 tick) is dropped in favour of the exact straddle test.

ready.description: When fading a breakout, risk about as much as the breakout run already made: the stop distance beyond the entry price is a fraction of the recent swing range.
ready.pseudocode: runSize = highest(high, runLookback)[0] - lowest(low, runLookback)[0]; ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= -runFraction * runSize * bigPointValue

complexity.reason: two fixed-length windows and a dollar conversion; the book's version needs a measured leg

catalog_match.note: Unrelated: AtrDollarsBelow is an entry filter on ATR in dollars. The catalog has no range-scaled protective stop.

ready.merge_notes: Brooks: 'risk about five points to make five points, expecting a test of the breakout' — the stop is sized to the move being faded. His measurement is the breakout's start-to-extreme run, which needs a leg measurement; the N-bar high-low range is the mechanizable stand-in and is what makes this an A/B rule rather than a C. Distinct from StopAtSignalBarRangeMultiple, which scales off ONE bar's range.

ready.description: Arm the breakeven stop only after the trade has held above the moving average for N consecutive bars since entry, rather than after a dollar profit.
ready.pseudocode: if (close[0] > ema(close, emaLength)[0]) barsAbove = barsAbove + 1; else barsAbove = 0; if (barsAbove >= barsAboveEma) armed = true; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && armed && close[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice()

complexity.reason: an EMA plus a consecutive-bar counter reset per position

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from BreakevenStop because the arming trigger is structural (a four-bar rally holding above the EMA) rather than a profit level; the two can arm on completely different bars, and the source itself flags the comparison for the authoring pass. XAverage has no register row yet; recorded as needed.

ready.description: A trade that went badly against you and then crawled back is worth scratching: once the open loss has exceeded a threshold at some point, exit as soon as price returns to the entry price.
ready.pseudocode:
// needs a minimum-position-profit tracker (the mirror of MaxPositionProfit); engine primitive request
if (ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < minProfitSoFar) minProfitSoFar = ctx.OpenPositionProfit(); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && minProfitSoFar <= -adverseDollars && close[0] >= ctx.EntryPrice()

complexity.reason: one running minimum of open profit, held per position, plus an entry-price comparison

catalog_match.note: The catalog's exit family is all peak-profit-side (ProfitProtector, TrailingStop); nothing reads maximum adverse excursion.

ready.merge_notes: Both sources describe a scaled-in position bought back at the first entry price; without pyramiding both reduce to the same thing, an exit at breakeven after a bad excursion. V21-02 states only the second half ('once the market gets back to their very first entry, they exit'), which on its own fires on the first profitable bar and is degenerate; T15-50's adverse-excursion gate is what makes the rule real, so T15-50's definition wins and V21-02 is a citation. ENGINE PRIMITIVE REQUEST: a MinPositionProfit accessor mirroring MaxPositionProfit. Until it exists the rule needs a hand-rolled running minimum in a persistent variable, which is why it is B and not A.

ready.description: Widen the protective stop to a multiple of the trade's normal initial risk: for spike entries taken without a pullback, and for a position that has moved against you and is being given room before it reverses.
ready.pseudocode:
// needs a fixed initial-risk accessor: the entry-to-initial-stop distance frozen at entry
ctx.MarketPosition() != 0 && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() <= -stopMultiple * initialRiskDollars

complexity.reason: the engine has no fixed initial-stop / initial-risk accessor; the entry-to-stop distance would have to be captured at entry by whichever stop rule set it

catalog_match.note: StopLoss with the dollar amount expressed as a multiple of the trade's own initial risk instead of a constant. With a constant risk per trade the two coincide, which is the cheap way to test this before the accessor exists.

ready.merge_notes: Both sources state a stop as a multiple of the normal one: V24-41 'entering in spikes requires a wider stop' (a stray, absorbed), V19-13 'traders will often double the size of the protective stop' after an adverse move. KEPT AT B FOR THE MISSING ACCESSOR, as briefed: the engine exposes no frozen initial-stop price, so a multiple of the entry-to-stop distance is not computable. Cross-reference: exits_targets merged the R-multiple PROFIT targets under ProfitTargetAtInitialRiskMultiple and hits the same gap — one accessor unblocks both, and R10-15 (a target at 1R) was sent there rather than duplicated here. The second half of V19-13, 'plan to reverse the position if the widened stop is hit', is already the catalog's FlatOrOpenLossExceeds and is not carried. V19-13's adverse-move precondition adds nothing: a stop only matters once price is against you.

ready.description: Take profit at a test of the trend's most recent swing extreme (the prior high for a long) -- the pullback trader's standard target, and the level a gap-bar swing or a wedge reversal is expected to reach.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= swingHigh(pivotStrength) - toleranceAtr * WFSafe_AvgTrueRange(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: needs a confirmed swing pivot at a variable distance back

catalog_match.note: The window approximation highest(high, N)[1] (T10-24's own note) would be CloseAbovePriorHighestHigh in Exit role; the book's level is a confirmed pivot, which can sit further back than any fixed N.

ready.merge_notes: Three statements of one target: the flag-pullback exit at the trend's extreme (V07-10), the double-top-bear-flag profit take at the last swing high (T10-24), and the first-moving-average-gap-bar swing target at the trend's prior extreme (R14-06, a stray sent from another bucket -- absorbed, it is a target). T10-24 supplies the ATR tolerance; V07-10's stallTicks 0 is the same parameter at zero. R14-06's follow-on 'expect a two-legged correction' is not part of the exit and is left to leg_counting.

ready.description: After a breakout of the session's opening range, exit when price reaches the opening-range extreme plus a multiple of the opening range's height -- the 'approximate doubling of the day's range'.
ready.pseudocode: orHigh = highest(high, openingBars) as of the openingBars-th bar of the session; orLow = the matching lowest(low, openingBars); target = orHigh + multiple * (orHigh - orLow); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target

complexity.reason: per-session opening-range state reset on each new date, then a fixed projection

ready.merge_notes: TP4-05 and T22-05 are the same rule in two chapters (Part IV intro and Trending Trading Range Days); TP4-05 supplies the openingBars parameter, T22-05 the 'doubling of the day's range' phrasing. Kept apart from PatternHeightMeasuredMoveTarget because the reference window is session-anchored (the first N bars of the day) rather than the N bars before the breakout -- different bars, and intraday-only.

ready.description: On a trading-range day, a reversal from near the day's extreme is expected to at least test the midpoint of the session's range so far; exit the countertrend long there.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= (sessionHigh + sessionLow) / 2

complexity.reason: running session high/low state, reset on each new date

ready.merge_notes: The one target in the bucket measured off the session's own developing range rather than a pattern; no restatements found. Brooks's paired warning (do not take swing profits early on a range day, since the opposite extreme is often taken out) is advice, not a condition.

ready.description: Gate: permit the signal only once price is within a tolerance of a measured-move target. Brooks's use is countertrend -- trade only with the trend until the market reaches the measured move, then look for fades there.
ready.pseudocode: target = highest(high, refBars)[k] + (highest(high, refBars)[k] - lowest(low, refBars)[k]); abs(high[0] - target) <= nearTargetAtr * WFSafe_AvgTrueRange(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: re-derives the measured-move target inside an entry rule (entry and exit panes share no state)

ready.merge_notes: R08-14 (countertrend entries allowed only in the measured-move area) and T03-17 (the measured-move level as one of the 'test' levels, a two-sided tolerance band) are one filter; R08-14's ATR tolerance beats T03-17's fixed toleranceTicks. T22-06 is the same proximity test used to BLOCK further with-trend breakout entries near the target; that is this filter negated, i.e. the per-placement toggle, so it is not a second rule -- but T22-06's own framing ('the market transitions into a second trading range') is research-grade and is not what is mechanized here. Brooks's caveat (p78): being at a measured move is not by itself a reason to fade; the pane system supplies the second reason by AND-ing another entry rule.

ready.description: Take profit once open profit reaches a multiple of THIS trade's own initial risk -- the distance from the entry price to the protective stop as it stood at entry. Brooks's scalp is 1x, his swing 2x or better.
ready.pseudocode: initialRisk = abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPriceCapturedAtEntry) * bigPointValue; ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * initialRisk

complexity.reason: trivial arithmetic, but it needs the initial stop distance captured once at entry and never overwritten by later stop-tightening

catalog_match.note: TakeProfitWithRatioStop drives both legs off one fixed dollar target; this scales the target off the trade's own realized initial stop distance, which varies with the placement's stop rule.

ready.merge_notes: Six statements of one rule at two parameter values: 1x for scalps and trading-range trades (RP2-10, R21-01, R24-04) and 2x for swings (R24-05, R30-01, T18-26). Brooks explicitly distinguishes the two styles, but they differ only in riskMultiple, so this is one rule with a parameter; default 1.0, his most-repeated floor. **Blocked on an accessor the engine lacks**: there is no ctx.InitialStopPrice() -- the stop distance in force at entry is not exposed, so the rule needs either that accessor or an input that restates the placement's stop distance. Kept B for that reason, not C: the definition itself is unambiguous. R21-01 also reads as TakeProfitWithRatioStop(ratio=1) with the trading-range rationale attached.

ready.description: Exit a with-trend position opened during a micro channel as soon as the channel breaks -- the first bar that violates the run of higher lows ends the tight momentum.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && microChannelRunLength[1] >= minBars && low[0] < low[1]

complexity.reason: a persistent run counter (the micro-channel primitive) plus a one-bar violation test

ready.merge_notes: Same shape as ExitOnFirstOppositeBodyAfterRun (a run, then the first bar that breaks it) but the run is counted on higher lows rather than bull bodies, so they fire on different bars; both listed on each other. Depends on whatever micro-channel counter the lines_channels bucket settles on -- a persistent counter, not pivot detection, so B rather than C.

ready.description: Exit at a projected trend-channel line: the parallel of the trend line through the swing lows, anchored at the intervening swing high. widthMultiple 1.0 exits at the channel line itself (with-trend breakouts of a channel usually fail); 2.0 gives the Andrew's-pitchfork target one further channel width beyond the midline.
ready.pseudocode: trendLine = line through the last two swing lows; channelLine = parallel anchored at the intervening swing high; level = trendLine.at(0) + widthMultiple * (channelLine.at(0) - trendLine.at(0)); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= level

complexity.reason: two swing pivots and a projected line value on every bar

ready.merge_notes: One rule at two parameter values. T21-24 exits when the high overshoots the channel line (widthMultiple 1.0); T26-08's pitchfork projection is a parallel as far beyond the middle line as the middle line is from the far boundary, i.e. the same construction at widthMultiple 2.0. Merging them by the width parameter is the whole reason they are not two rules. Overlaps the lines_channels bucket's channel-line primitive; kept here because both candidates are exits.

ready.description: Waning momentum: the gains between successive swing highs are shrinking (the newest increment is less than a fraction of the one before). Take profits on longs.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && swingHigh(strength)[1] > swingHigh(strength)[2] && (swingHigh(strength)[1] - swingHigh(strength)[2]) < shrinkFraction * (swingHigh(strength)[2] - swingHigh(strength)[3])

complexity.reason: three consecutive swing highs

ready.merge_notes: Brooks's worked numbers (second peak eight ticks above the first, third only three above the second) give shrinkFraction well under 0.5; 0.5 kept as the candidate's default. Also usable as a negative entry filter, which is the per-placement negate toggle, not a second rule.

ready.description: Target the trade's profit at a fraction of the market's own typical recent pullback: if the last pullback ran about fifteen ticks, look to exit ten to fifteen ticks up from the low.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= entrySwingLow + profitFraction * priorPullbackSize

complexity.reason: arithmetic on a remembered pullback measurement captured at entry

catalog_match.note: The same shape with the market's last pullback in place of the ATR as the distance measure.

ready.merge_notes: B because 'the most recent pullback size' needs the prior swing high and low; if that is approximated by highest(high, N) - lowest(low, N) it collapses into PatternHeightMeasuredMoveTarget at a fractional multiple, which is worth checking at authoring time.

ready.description: Brooks's bar counting, the H1/H2/H3/H4 and L1/L2/L3/L4 family. A persistent count of completed pullback legs since the trend last made a fresh resetLookback-bar high. A bar whose high exceeds the prior bar's high advances the count, but only once a new low has formed since the last counted bar (otherwise it is a retest of the same leg, not a new one); the count resets to 0 the instant the close makes a fresh resetLookback-bar high. Fires on the bar that advances the count to countTarget - that bar is the high-N signal bar, and under the corpus's stop-entry convention (signal-bar close, next-bar open) the fire IS the entry. Mirror: low 1..low 4.

complexity.reason: a cross-bar counter plus two remembered prices and one Highest window; no pivot detection and no lookahead

catalog_match.note: nothing in the catalog holds cross-bar counter state of this kind

ready.merge_notes: Twenty-three statements of one primitive, the single most load-bearing rule in the trilogy. THE DEFINITION THAT WINS IS R17-01 (Ranges ch17), for the reason MERGE.md gives: it needs no swing pivots, no lookahead and no leg definition - a bar advances the count on a higher high only after a new low since the last counted bar, and the count resets on a fresh N-bar high. Every other definition here is a citation, not a rule. The losing definitions, in the order they cost more machinery: (a) swing-pivot leg segmentation - R05-17, V24-03, TP1-05, T18-02, T20-02, V01-05, all graded hard and all needing SwingHigh/SwingLow plus pivot retention; (b) 'count each higher-high bar since the pullback began, resetting when the trend makes a new extreme' with the extreme left undefined - R00-61's R00-60, T00-20's T00-19, TP1-06 (this is R17-01 minus the concrete reset, which is exactly what R17-01 sharpens); (c) the ad hoc per-chapter counters T10-23 (reset on a new trend high, resetLookback 20 - the closest independent restatement of R17-01, and strong corroboration), T15-19 (resetOnNewHighBars 10), T21-72 (maxPullbackBars 20). The 'at least one bar that did not make a higher high between counts' phrasing (T10-23, T15-19, T21-72) is behaviourally the same guard as R17-01's 'a new low since the last counted bar' in a real pullback, but R17-01's is the cheaper and less ambiguous test and is the one carried. countTarget covers high 1 (R05-18, V00-52, R17-03, R01-09's 'first pullback', V01-10's pullback ordinal), high 2 (the most-stated setup: R05-19, V00-53, R17-04, T10-23, T15-19, T18-02, T20-02, T21-72, V01-05, TP1-06, T00-20, R00-61), high 3 (wedge bull flag) and high 4 (R17-06); Brooks caps the count at 4 and the counter saturates there. resetLookback defaults differ (R17-01/T10-23 20, T15-19 10, T21-72 20); 20 is carried. ABC corrections are this counter under another name - leg A is the run to count 1, leg B the failed bounce, leg C the run to count 2 - so no separate rule (R00-61, R17-01 and T01-05 all say so). ROLL-UP: swing_structure merged R17-01 alone under this same key with the same shape; the two entries are the same rule and only one should be authored. countTarget was added there for the same reason it is added here - a rule must fire on something. Folded the swing_structure copy (R17-01), the same persistent counter from the same source.

ready.description: The current pullback has completed AT LEAST minLegs legs - HighLowBarCount's counter read as a threshold rather than an equality. Brooks's 'a pullback, like all trends, will commonly have at least two legs': a with-trend entry is favoured only once the count has reached two.
ready.pseudocode: count >= minLegs   // the counter of HighLowBarCount, same state and same reset

complexity.reason: the HighLowBarCount counter with a >= comparison

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from HighLowBarCount deliberately: == countTarget fires on ONE bar (the signal bar) while >= minLegs stays true for the rest of the pullback, so as a context filter ANDed into a pane they select different bars. All three sources state it as a context/quality read, not an entry: RP3-03 'a pullback commonly has at least two legs, fade the first leg's breakout and wait for the second'; V01-03 'it was two-legged, so the bears showed some strength' (its swing-pivot countLegs is the losing definition, replaced by the R17-01 counter); T19-21 'repeated two-legged pullbacks are setting up with-trend entries' - the REPETITION across successive pullbacks is dropped as having no bar-level test, so T19-21 is carried lossily as the single-pullback reading. Default 2 from all three.

ready.description: The pullback in progress has lasted no more than maxPullbackBars bars, measured as the bars since the trend last made a fresh resetLookback-bar high (the same anchor HighLowBarCount resets on). A brief pullback is Brooks's sign of strength; NEGATED, the rule is his sign of weakness ('the pullback extends for several bars').
ready.pseudocode: barsSince(close[0] > highest(high, resetLookback)[1]) <= maxPullbackBars

complexity.reason: a bars-since counter keyed on the same fresh-extreme test HighLowBarCount already computes

ready.merge_notes: One rule and the per-placement negate toggle. R02-15 / T00-34 / V00-49 are the strength form (<= 2 bars); R02-24 is the same test negated at a different threshold (>= 4 bars, weakness). Both book values recorded, default 2 (three sources against one). R02-15's and V00-49's second conjunct - 'and it follows a bar that is not a strong bear reversal bar' - is NOT carried here: bar_anatomy_reversal_signal already merged it as PullbackNotAfterStrongOppositeReversalBar, and the pane ANDs it. The anchor is the design decision that lets this leave research grade: the sources say 'the pullback' without saying when it started, and the fresh-N-bar-high reset from R17-01 supplies a concrete start with no pivot search. R11-11 (dropped) states the same measure as a WINDOW, 5 to 10 bars, for a high 2 - if the authoring pass wants a band, minPullbackBars is the second input to add.

ready.description: The first pullback bar after a breakout does not arrive until at least minBarsBeforePullback bars have passed since the breakout bar: the current bar is the first bar since the breakout whose low is below the prior bar's low, and it is at least N bars after it. Brooks's leading sign of breakout strength; NEGATED it is his sign of weakness ('the first pullback occurs two bars after the reversal').
ready.pseudocode:
b = barsSince(close[0] > highest(high, breakoutLookback)[1]);
b >= minBarsBeforePullback && low[0] < low[1] && lowest(low, b)[1] >= low[1]   // no earlier pullback bar since the breakout

complexity.reason: a bars-since-breakout counter plus a 'no earlier pullback bar' window test

ready.merge_notes: Eight statements of one test, five of them the same sentence copied across books ('The first pullback occurs only after three or more bars of breaking out' - R00-58, R02-14, V00-48, T00-33). Three add something. R05-02 is the same rule at minBarsBeforePullback = 0/1: it is the bare marker 'the first bar since the breakout with a low below the prior bar's low', which is where the 'no earlier pullback bar' clause in the pseudocode comes from and is the most mechanizable phrasing of the first-pullback anchor. R02-23 is the rule NEGATED (a pullback within 2 bars = weakness) - the per-placement toggle, both thresholds recorded. T15-40 is the OTHER bound, 'any pullback should come within five bars or so' - negated at minBarsBeforePullback = 6; its raceBars conjunct (consecutive higher highs since the breakout) is bar_anatomy_trend_doji's ConsecutiveTrendBars and is ANDed by the pane, not carried. V02-13 is the one source that mechanizes the anchor fully - 'the first down-close since a bull reversal bar k bars ago with k-1 up closes between' - and is the reason the grade is moderate rather than research; its anchor is a reversal bar rather than a breakout, which is a placement choice, not a different rule. Default 3, unanimous among the sources that state it. The breakout anchor uses the same fresh-N-bar-extreme test as HighLowBarCount so the two share one window.

ready.description: The high 1 in a strong bull spike: after spikeBars consecutive bull trend bars, the first bar whose low is below the prior bar's low is the signal bar, and the entry fires when a bar within maxWaitBars closes above that signal bar's high. Mirror: the low 1 after a bear spike.

complexity.reason: a 'spike seen, first pullback seen' state pair carried across an unknown number of bars, plus one retained price

catalog_match.note: the trigger term is CloseAbovePriorHigh against a RETAINED signal-bar high rather than a fixed lag, which the catalog rule cannot express

ready.merge_notes: Kept as a composite because it is a named Brooks setup ('buying a high 1 pullback in a strong bull spike', stated in all three) AND because the trigger is against a bar at a VARIABLE lag - the pane cannot AND CloseAbovePriorHigh(fixed lag) with a spike filter and get this. It is NOT HighLowBarCount at countTarget 1: this rule's reset is a completed spike, not a fresh N-bar high, and its trigger is a later bar closing over a retained level rather than the signal bar itself. spikeBars: T07-45 says 3, TP3-16 says 4, T23-04 says 3 - default 3. T23-04 is the same mechanism anchored at the session open ('trend from the open'), so its placement is INTRADAY-ONLY while the rule itself is not; the always-in / trend-from-open flag it also reads is a context_regime rule the pane ANDs. Brooks's caveat in TP3-16 and T07-45, 'but not after a buy climax', is PostClimaxCorrectionBlock and is ANDed, not carried here.

ready.description: The second entry: an earlier same-side signal triggered within the last withinBars bars, that first entry failed (price traded back beyond the first signal bar's opposite extreme), and a new same-side signal is triggering now. Brooks's most-repeated reliability filter, and the one condition he says is sufficient on its own.
ready.pseudocode: exists k in 2..withinBars: close[k] > high[k+1] && lowest(low, k-1)[0] < low[k+1] && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: a bounded backward scan with two conditions per candidate bar; no pattern registry and no per-placement state

catalog_match.note: LastTradeCooldown gates on a REALIZED trade's outcome via PositionProfit/BarsSinceExit; this gates on a repeated raw pattern whether or not a trade was taken, and can fire before any trade exists

ready.merge_notes: Eight statements, and the fork that matters is what 'the same logic as the first signal' means. TWO OPTIONS were on the table. (1) A generic setup-identity registry - 'the same Entry candidate fired and failed' - which is what R00-52, V00-65, T00-21, T06-31 and R26-06 describe, all graded research, and which needs engine support the corpus does not have (a per-placement fire/fail log). (2) T21-28's CONCRETE PROXY: define the signal as the generic price trigger (a close above the prior bar's high) and the failure as price trading back below that signal bar's low, then scan the last withinBars bars for one. T21-28 WINS - it is a bounded scan over prices, needs no registry, and reproduces the second entry Brooks actually points at in the figures. It is lossy in exactly one way, and the loss should be recorded: it counts a second GENERIC trigger, not a second instance of whichever pattern is placed alongside it. Option 1 stays available if per-placement signal memory is ever added; bar_anatomy_reversal_signal reached the same conclusion for SecondReversalSignal and its 'track only the engine's own last Entry signal' decision is the third option. withinBars: T21-28 10, V24-18 8, V00-65 5, T06-31 10, R00-52 6, R26-06 10 - default 10. V04-13 is this filter with a climax anchor ('buy a higher low after a sell climax, not the initial reversal'), carried as a citation; the climax term is ANDed. Near-miss kept separate: SecondSignalNotBetterPrice is the price-quality gate ON this rule, not a restatement of it.

ready.description: A triggered high-N long (low-N short) fails: after HighLowBarCount reached countTarget, price trades back beyond the signal bar's opposite extreme. Brooks reads a failed high 4 / low 4 as the side losing control, and permits or takes the reversal trade in the other direction.
ready.pseudocode:
countReached = HighLowBarCount fired at countTarget on bar k;
close[0] < signalLow[k]   // long side failed -> permit/take the short

complexity.reason: the HighLowBarCount counter plus its already-retained signalLow and a bars-since cap

ready.merge_notes: Six statements of one event and its consequence. The event is identical in all six - a high-N or low-N setup triggered and then price went back through the signal bar - and the machinery is already inside HighLowBarCount (signalLow is retained there, so the failure test is free). countTarget default 4, the case Brooks names most (R00-62, V00-55, T00-48 all say low 4); T04-08 states it at 1 (fading a failed low 1 in a bottoming bear trend) and VP1-11 at 2/3 (a failed low 2 as a failed bear flag), so the same input covers all of them. Two sources add a conjunct that is NOT carried and is ANDed by the pane instead: T00-48 requires a bear trend-line break before the bears count as having regained control (a lines_channels_trendlines rule; TLValue recorded in el_words_needed for it), and VP1-11 requires the resulting breakout in the new direction (a breakouts rule). T00-48's framing is the negate toggle on this rule - block with-trend entries while the failure stands - so it needs no second rule. R00-62's 'wait for more price action' is advice with no test and is dropped from the reading.

ready.description: Exit (and optionally reverse) the open position the moment the OPPOSITE side's bar count reaches countTarget. Brooks: 'if you ever buy early, always get out and even reverse if the market triggers a low 2 or 3 short'; mirrored for a short caught by a high 2 or 3.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && lowCount == countTarget

complexity.reason: the same counter as HighLowBarCount read on the opposite side, plus a position test

catalog_match.note: the catalog rule is an Entry-side reversal permission keyed on dollars; this is an Exit keyed on the opposing count triggering

ready.merge_notes: ROLL-UP: swing_structure merged V21-04 ('countertrend traders trying to buy in a bear trend should always exit on a low 2 signal') under this same key with the same shape - one rule, two sources across two buckets, author once. Kept as its own rule rather than a placement of HighLowBarCount because it reads the OPPOSITE side's counter, which a mirrored Entry placement cannot supply, and because it is an Exit. R17-13's 'especially if there is a strong bear signal bar' is a bar_anatomy_reversal_signal term with no threshold given and is dropped; the 'optionally reverse' half is the engine's own reversal behaviour, not a condition. Folded the swing_structure copy (V21-04): the same exit on the opposing count reaching countTarget.

ready.description: Suppress a fresh high 1 that follows a completed high-1(s)-then-high-2 sequence without an intervening deeper pullback: the counter has just advanced to 1 again, and the PREVIOUS count cycle had already reached at least minPriorCount. Brooks: 'after a series of winning trades, be suspicious of renewed strength without first seeing a larger pullback - it might be a trap setting up.'
ready.pseudocode:
// one extra persistent value beside HighLowBarCount: prevCycleMaxCount, latched when the count resets
count == 1 && justAdvanced && prevCycleMaxCount >= minPriorCount

complexity.reason: one additional latched integer on top of the HighLowBarCount state

ready.merge_notes: Single source, mined as research grade because it appeared to need 'a memory of prior setup TYPES, a new kind of state'. Under R17-01's counter it does not: the sequence H1(,H1), H2, then H1 again IS the counter reaching >= 2, resetting on a fresh N-bar high, and re-advancing to 1, so one latched integer covers it. That is why it is B and not C. Used NEGATED it is the filter Brooks states ('it is wise to wait'), so the per-placement toggle gives both readings. The 'final flag' framing R11-24 references is a three_push_patterns concept and is not carried.

ready.description: The second leg of the correction has run beyond the first leg's extreme: the running low since the count reached 2 is below the low retained when the count reached 1 (mirror: the running high above the count-1 high). Brooks: 'bears who shorted the first up leg will add as soon as the second leg up goes above the high of the first leg up.'
ready.pseudocode: count >= 2 && minLowSince < signalLowAtCountOne   // both values already retained by HighLowBarCount

complexity.reason: one extra retained price on top of the HighLowBarCount state; the comparison itself is trivial

ready.merge_notes: Single source. Mined as hard because it was framed in terms of leg 1 and leg 2 identified by pivots; under R17-01's counter the two legs' extremes are the values the counter already keeps (signalLow at each advance, and the running minimum since), so no pivots are needed. This is the EXPANDING correction - distinct from LegCountAtLeast, which only asks how many legs there have been, and from HighLowBarCount, whose advance guard asks for a new low since the last COUNTED bar rather than beyond the FIRST leg's extreme. Those two coincide for a strictly deepening pullback and diverge for a shallow second leg, which is exactly the case Brooks is separating.

ready.description: Block with-trend entries for blockBars bars after consecutive buy climaxes: no run of climaxCount consecutive climactic bull moves has completed within the last blockBars bars. Brooks: 'after three consecutive sell climaxes the market usually corrects sideways to up for at least 10 bars and with at least two legs.'
ready.pseudocode: barsSince(ConsecutiveClimaxBars fired) > blockBars

complexity.reason: a bars-since counter keyed on an existing climax detector

ready.merge_notes: Four statements of one block, unanimous on 10 bars and on 'at least two legs' as the expected correction. All four were mined at hard or research grade because 'climax' had no definition; bar_anatomy_trend_doji has since merged ConsecutiveClimaxBars as an authorable rule, so the only thing left here is the bars-since counter - hence B, not C. climaxCount 3 from RP1-14 and R22-15 (T21-40 and T21-71 say 'consecutive climaxes' and 'a buy climax' without a count, so 3 is the stated value and 1 is the loose reading). T21-71 adds the useful specific: after a climax a high 1 and maybe a high 2 will fail, so the block should lift at count >= 2 - that is HighLowBarCount ANDed, not a second rule. R22-15's session scoping ('the third consecutive sell climax of the day') is a time_session concern and is dropped; the bar window does the same work without a session reset. Carried as a filter, so a placement that wants the opposite reading (fade after three climaxes) uses the negate toggle.

ready.description: Block new longs for blockBars bars after a failed new high: price closed above the highest high of the last N bars and then, within failBars bars, a bear trend bar closed back below that level. Brooks: assume the market trades down for at least a couple of legs and at least 10 bars.

complexity.reason: a retained breakout level, a bounded failure window and a countdown; the swing-high reference is replaced by the N-bar-extreme window

ready.merge_notes: Single source. Mined as hard on a swing-high reference; the fresh-N-bar-extreme window used elsewhere in this bucket replaces the pivot and drops it to moderate. The 10-bar, two-legged correction horizon is the same number PostClimaxCorrectionBlock carries, from a different trigger - kept separate because the trigger is a failed breakout, not a climax, and breakouts_pullback_retest owns the failure detector (FailedBreakoutReversal) that this could eventually be keyed on. TP3-23's other two outcomes on page 311 (enough follow-through = stay long; sideways = buy lower) are not conditions and are dropped.

ready.description: Price poked beyond the projected trend channel line within the last K bars and this bar closes back inside the channel as a reversal bar -- the countertrend fade at the channel line.
ready.pseudocode: lowest(low, overshootBars) < channelLine[0] && close[0] > channelLine[0] && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: the channel-line projection, evaluated across a small window

ready.merge_notes: Four statements of Brooks's single most-repeated channel trade. T14-04 and T15-15 are the same bar (poke beyond, close back inside, reversal body) with bodyFraction 0.5 and 0.6; 0.6 chosen. V02-21 lets the poke be up to three bars old (lowest(low, overshootBars) < line) and VP1-15 puts it exactly one bar back -- so overshootBars is the parameter and 1 the default, which reproduces T14-04/T15-15 exactly. Kept apart from ChannelLineBreakoutFailure: that one needs a prior bar to CLOSE beyond the line, this one only a wick.

ready.description: A large with-trend trend bar reaches the projected channel line -- the vacuum test. Brooks fades it: the eager buyers who created it are the last ones.
ready.pseudocode: high[0] >= channelLine[0] && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (high[0] - low[0]) >= largeBarAtrMultiple * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the channel-line projection plus a large-trend-bar test

ready.merge_notes: Stray sent here from bar_anatomy_trend_doji; it fits and is absorbed. Deliberately NOT merged into ChannelLineOvershootReversal even though both fade at the line: this bar closes WITH the trend and near its high, the reversal form closes back inside against it -- opposite bar shapes, different bars. The book's use is a fade, so the placement is the trend bar's opposite side; the authoring pass should note the sides read backwards from the bar's own colour.

ready.description: A bar within the last N CLOSED beyond a channel's line and this bar closes back inside the channel -- the failed channel breakout, which Brooks says then runs to the opposite side of the channel.
ready.pseudocode: exists i in 1..failBars with close[i] < channelLine[i] && close[0] > channelLine[0]

complexity.reason: the projected line evaluated on every bar of a small window

ready.merge_notes: Five statements, one behaviour, and all five give the same five-bar window -- the most consistent number in the bucket. They differ only in WHICH line broke: T03-16, V04-09 and T21-23 the trend channel line (a with-trend breakout that fails), T14-07 the bottom of a falling channel (which is that channel's channel line, despite the mined pseudocode calling it a trend line), T15-31 either side ('with ANY channel breakout that reenters the channel'). T15-31's generic statement wins as the definition and the line is a placement choice. Companion exit is ChannelLineTargetExit at the opposite line (T15-35).

ready.description: Exit the long when the bar's high reaches the projected channel line above -- take profit where the channel says the move should stall.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= channelLine[0] - touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the projected line, read while in a position

ready.merge_notes: Three framings of one exit. T15-14 is the with-trend long taking profit at the top of its own bull channel; T15-35 is the countertrend long from a failed breakout targeting the OPPOSITE side of the channel; R10-03 states the line as a magnet with no trade attached. Same bars once the line is a placement choice, so one rule. touchTolAtr defaults to 0 (T15-14); a small tolerance is the alternative Brooks implies by 'rallies up to that line'.

ready.description: The channel line is being penetrated now and it was already penetrated at least once in the last N bars -- prefer the second penetration to the first when fading a channel.
ready.pseudocode: high[0] > channelLine[0] && countIf(high[i] > channelLine[i], i in 1..lookback) >= 1

complexity.reason: a window count of a derived per-bar flag; hard only through the line it counts

ready.merge_notes: Brooks's 'especially if it is the second penetration that is reversing', which he attaches to the channel-line fade throughout both books. Kept separate from ChannelLineOvershootReversal so the fade can be tested with and without it -- that is exactly the comparison Brooks is asserting.

ready.description: A bar closes beyond the channel line with a strong with-trend body -- not a reversal, a strengthening trend. The filter against fading a channel-line break.
ready.pseudocode: close[0] > channelLine[0] && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

complexity.reason: the projected line plus a trend-bar body test

ready.merge_notes: V04-10 states the routing rule with no numbers ('breaking a trend channel line means the trend has increased in strength', the opposite implication to a trend-line break); V10-04 gives it the measurable form -- the bar must CLOSE well beyond the line with a strong body. V10-04 wins, V04-10 is the citation. Direct contrast with ChannelLineOvershootReversal: same line, opposite bar shape, opposite trade, so both are kept.

ready.description: Some bar in the last N overshot the channel line by at least K x ATR -- a SIGNIFICANT overshoot, as opposed to a minor poke. Brooks uses it negated: a trend with no significant overshoots is healthy.
ready.pseudocode: exists k in 0..lookback-1 with (high[k] - channelLine[k]) >= significantOvershootAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the projected line on every bar of a window, plus an ATR magnitude

ready.merge_notes: The same sign-of-strength bullet, stated identically in the glossary (T00-45) and in the trends chapter on trend strength (T19-19). Both are phrased as the NEGATIVE ('no significant overshoots occur'), which is the per-placement toggle; the rule states the positive. Not ChannelLineOvershoot with a window: the ATR magnitude that separates 'significant' from 'minor' is the content, and it is the miners' number, not Brooks's. The sources' second clause -- 'and the minor ones result in only sideways corrections' -- has no measurable form and is dropped.

ready.description: The channel's width (channel line minus trend line) is narrower now than K bars ago by at least a fraction -- a converging channel, i.e. a wedge or triangle. Negated and inverted it is the expanding triangle.
ready.pseudocode: widthNow = channelLine[0] - trendLine[0]; widthEarlier = channelLine[k] - trendLine[k]; widthNow <= convergeFraction * widthEarlier

complexity.reason: both projected lines evaluated at two points in time

ready.merge_notes: Direction-agnostic (a width is a width), so sides are 'same'. Brooks's own framing -- parallel means continuation, convergent means wedge, divergent means expanding triangle -- makes this the cheap wedge detector; the three_push_patterns bucket carries the pivot-based one (T14-08), and the authoring pass should compare them.

ready.description: The close sits in the lower fraction of the channel -- above the trend line by no more than F x the channel height. Buy low in the channel, and the odds fall as price works into the upper half.
ready.pseudocode: close[0] <= trendLine[0] + fraction * (channelLine[0] - trendLine[0])

complexity.reason: both projected lines; the horizontal proxy is trivial but is a different rule

catalog_match.note: T15-23's HORIZONTAL proxy -- close below the Donchian midline (highest + lowest)/2 -- is AtrBandBreakout at atrMultiple 0 with the sides flipped, i.e. already in the corpus. The SLOPING form here is not: its midline follows the channel, not a flat Donchian.

ready.merge_notes: Only the sloping form is carried as a rule; the horizontal proxy the miner offered alongside it is already authorable as AtrBandBreakout(atrMultiple = 0) flipped, and should not be authored again. Brooks p256: the middle of the channel has a magnetic pull, so a band form (lower third, upper third) is a reasonable second parameterization of the same rule.
