ready.description: There is at least F x the channel height between the current close and the channel line ahead -- room for the trade to pay before it hits the far side of the channel.
ready.pseudocode: (channelLine[0] - close[0]) >= minRoomFraction * (channelLine[0] - trendLine[0])

complexity.reason: both projected lines

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from PriceInLowerHalfOfChannel although both measure position within the channel: this one is scaled to the channel's own height as a trade-viability test ('so tight there was no room for a profitable short and no trade should be taken'), the other places price in the channel for direction. An absolute form (room >= minRoomAtr x ATR) is the alternative the miner flagged and is the better one if channel height turns out to be noisy.

ready.description: A recent bar tested the channel's near line and price has since moved a fixed ATR amount back away from that test bar's extreme -- a with-trend momentum entry off the line test.
ready.pseudocode: exists k in 1..testWindow with low[k] <= trendLine[k] + touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength); close[0] >= low[k] + moveAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the projected line across a window, plus the test bar's extreme carried forward

ready.merge_notes: Brooks states it as the bears' mirror ('short on a fixed amount below every test of the top of the channel, like one or two points down'); the long side written here is the mirror of that. The 'one or two points' is Emini-specific and is carried as moveAtr so it ports.

ready.description: Exit when price reaches the level where the channel began -- the low of the pullback that followed the spike. Brooks's standing minimum target for any move against a spike-and-channel trend.
ready.pseudocode: channelStart = lowest(low, pullbackBars) as of the bar the channel was confirmed; ctx.MarketPosition() < 0 && low[0] <= channelStart + toleranceAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: one remembered price level, but remembering it requires the spike-to-channel boundary

ready.merge_notes: Seven statements of the same target, the most-repeated idea in the bucket. T21-13 supplies the level definition that wins -- channelStart = the lowest low of the pullback that followed the spike -- because it is the only one that says how to compute it; T15-45, T21-42, R18-07, R10-04 and V04-18 all just assert the level gets tested. TWO ANCHOR READINGS exist and Brooks uses both loosely: the pullback low after the spike (T21-13, T15-45 'the beginning of the channel where they began buying') and the SPIKE TOP itself (R05-22 'it usually tests down to the top of the spike, and eventually to the bottom of the channel', R18-07 'the high following bar 1'). The pullback low is chosen; R05-22's spike top is the shallower of the two and can be a second parameterization if the deeper one proves too far. V04-18's 'within a day or two' bar count is dropped -- it does not convert across timeframes and the target does not need it.

ready.description: Price has come back down to the channel's starting level and a bar closes above the prior bar's high there -- buy the test of the start of the channel.
ready.pseudocode: low[1] <= channelStart + tolAtr * atr(atrLength) && low[1] >= channelStart - maxUndershootAtr * atr(atrLength) && close[0] > high[1]

ready.merge_notes: The entry side of ChannelStartRetestExit's level. ready.merge_notes: Kept here rather than sent to exits_targets because the content is a channel property ('the height of the channel is often about the same as the height of the spike'), but the miner's own note says the arithmetic is identical to the spike measured-move target R07-02, which lives in exits_targets. ready.description: Three consecutive higher swing highs have formed since the channel began -- the third push, after which Brooks will look for a channel reversal or downside breakout.
ready.pseudocode: swingHigh(1).price > swingHigh(2).price && swingHigh(2).price > swingHigh(3).price && all three formed after channelStartBar

ready.merge_notes: The same primitive stated in both channel chapters with the same count of three. ready.description: At least three consecutive swing legs each making a higher swing low AND a higher swing high, where each breakout retraces back past its own breakout point before the next leg -- Brooks's stairs, a broad channel trend.
ready.pseudocode: for k in 1..minStairs-1: swingLow(k).price > swingLow(k+1).price && swingHigh(k).price > swingHigh(k+1).price && swingLow(k).price < swingHigh(k+1).price (the overlap)

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection, a run test over several pivots, and an overlap test between consecutive legs

ready.merge_notes: The only source in the trilogy that defines stairs precisely enough to code, and the chapter named for it. The overlap requirement is what separates stairs from a plain trend of higher highs and higher lows, and from an accelerating spike-and-channel; it is carried. Gates StairsBreakoutFade, StairsPullbackLimitEntry and ShrinkingStairs.

ready.description: Each successive new extreme in a stairs trend extends less than the one before it -- shrinking stairs, a waning-momentum filter against the next with-trend breakout.
ready.pseudocode: (swingHigh(1).price - swingHigh(2).price) < (swingHigh(2).price - swingHigh(3).price) && (swingHigh(2).price - swingHigh(3).price) < (swingHigh(3).price - swingHigh(4).price)

complexity.reason: four swing pivots and a monotonic-decrease test over the gaps between them

ready.merge_notes: T00-17 is the glossary entry over four pivots, T26-04 (stray, absorbed) the chapter statement over two legs; one rule with shrinkLegs as the parameter, default 3 comparisons (four pivots) from T00-17. Kept apart from StairsPattern: a stairs trend can have growing, equal or shrinking steps, and only the shrinking case carries the warning.

ready.description: In a stairs trend, buy a fixed distance below the most recent swing low -- the pullback that tests the prior stair.
ready.pseudocode: stairsDetected && low[0] <= swingLow(1).price - stairPullbackAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: the stairs primitive plus the most recent swing pivot

ready.merge_notes: Brooks's 'four points below the prior swing low' is instrument-specific; carried as an ATR multiple so it ports, with the point form as the alternative. This is DipBelowPriorBarLow's idea applied to a swing pivot rather than the prior bar, which is why it is a separate rule -- different level, different bars.

ready.description: At least minBreaks trend-line breaks have occurred in the last withinBars bars: the standing permission for a countertrend entry. Brooks's single most repeated rule -- never trade against a trend until its trend line has broken.
ready.pseudocode: countTrue( close[k] > bearTlValueAt(k) for k in 0..withinBars-1 ) >= minBreaks

complexity.reason: the projected line must be evaluated at every bar in the window, with the pivots as they stood on that bar

ready.merge_notes: Behaviourally distinct from TrendLineBreak: that one fires only on the break bar, this one stays true for a window afterwards, which is what every one of these nine candidates actually wants. Book lookbacks: 20 (TP4-10, T21-81, TP3-09), 30 (R08-15), 60 (V02-28); default 20. V02-28 ('prior breaks of earlier bear trend lines, this isn't the first sign of strength') is this rule at minBreaks >= 2, so it is a parameter, not a rule. R17-02 ('at least a tiny trend line break between the high 1 and the high 2') is the same test at swingStrength 1 with withinBars = bars since the last counted signal; the count gating it is the decided HighLowBarCount counter (R17-01, leg_counting). The mining files themselves flag TP4-10 and T21-81 as the same rule.

ready.description: In a bull trend, the bar dips to (or slightly through) the projected bull trend line and closes back above it -- the with-trend pullback buy at the line. Mirrored for a bear trend line.
ready.pseudocode: bullTl0 = tlValue(low[p1b], p1b, low[p2b], p2b, 0) using the last two confirmed swing lows; low[0] <= bullTl0 + touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength) && close[0] > bullTl0

complexity.reason: needs the projected line value at the current bar; the test itself is one comparison

ready.merge_notes: T13-03 and T15-13 are the same setup written twice (the ch13 file says so); T21-20 is the same test inside a spike-and-channel. R10-02 states only the proximity half ('trend lines are magnets') -- the weaker definition, folded in as a citation; the close-back-above term is kept because every trading statement has it. R28-38 places a limit order AT the line rather than a stop above the reversal bar; under the standing signal-bar-close / next-bar-open convention both mechanize to the same bar, so one rule. Brooks (T15-13, p273) notes ~80% of pokes below a bull channel line fail, which is why the poke-and-close-back form is the default rather than a pure touch.

ready.description: Price has touched (come within touchTolAtr of) the projected trend line at least minTouches times in the last windowBars bars without drifting more than maxDistanceAtr from it -- bars hugging the line, which Brooks reads as an imminent break (or, less often, an acceleration).

complexity.reason: the projected line evaluated at every bar of the window plus a touch counter and a running max distance

ready.merge_notes: One condition stated three ways. Book windows: 'five to 10 bars close to the line' (V22-04, minTouches 5), 'repeatedly tests in a relatively small number of bars' (T13-08, minTouches 4 over 20), T21-59 minTouches 4 over 40. Default 4 over 20. T21-59 also adds the entry trigger ('buy when a bar closes through the line'), which is TrendLineBreak ANDed in the pane, and contributes the maxDistanceAtr containment term kept here because both V22-04 and T13-08 describe the same 'cannot drift far from the line' quality. Direction of the resolution is deliberately NOT encoded: Brooks says break (usually) or accelerate, so this stays a filter.

ready.description: A second failed attempt to hold beyond the line: an earlier bar in the window already tested the projected line and reversed off it, and this bar tests it and reverses again -- the second-entry principle applied to a line test rather than to a bar pattern.
ready.pseudocode: reversedAtLine(i) = abs(low[i] - bullTlValueAt(i)) <= touchTolAtr * atr(atrLength) && close[i] > bullTlValueAt(i); countTrue( reversedAtLine(i) for i in 2..maxBarsBetween ) >= 1 && reversedAtLine(0)

complexity.reason: the per-bar line test from TrendLineTouch evaluated over a window, plus the second-occurrence counter

ready.merge_notes: Not a composition of TrendLineTouch with anything: the two touches are at different bars, which the AND-ing pane system cannot express, so it must be its own rule. Distinct from TrendLineTouchCount, which counts bars NEAR the line regardless of whether each one reversed; listed on both.

ready.description: The trend line drawn through the two most recent swing pivots is flatter than the one drawn through the pivot pair before it -- successive trend lines losing slope, which Brooks reads as a maturing, weakening trend.
ready.pseudocode: p1b = swingLowBar(swingStrength, 3); p2b = swingLowBar(swingStrength, 2); p3b = swingLowBar(swingStrength, 1); newSlope = (low[p3b] - low[p2b]) / (p2b - p3b); oldSlope = (low[p2b] - low[p1b]) / (p1b - p2b); oldSlope > 0 && newSlope < flattenFraction * oldSlope

complexity.reason: three confirmed swing pivots and two slopes; no persistent redraw history is needed once 'the current line is the newest pivot pair' is the construction rule

ready.merge_notes: The mined candidate was graded research because it assumed a persisted history of redrawn lines and a rule for when a 'redraw' happens. The construction decision removes that: the current line is always the newest confirmed pivot pair, so the prior line is the pair one pivot back and the comparison is three pivots wide. Downgraded from research to hard on that basis.

ready.description: A bar pokes through a micro trend line (a line across two pivots inside the last microLineBars bars, detected at strength 1) and the market closes back through that bar's own extreme within failureWindowBars -- the failed micro-breakout entry back in the micro-trend's direction.
ready.pseudocode: microTl = tlValue over the last two strength-1 swing highs with p2b - p1b <= microLineBars; high[1] > microTl(1) && close[0] < low[1]

complexity.reason: the same pivot/projection machinery at strength 1 over a short window, plus the failure test

ready.merge_notes: T16-08 is the construction (a citation: the same TrendLineBreak machinery at microSwingStrength 1 and a <= microLineBars pivot span), T16-09 the entry, R00-39 the front-matter statement of the same setup, V07-02 the same failure reclassified as a one-bar final flag. Kept apart from TrendLineBreak: a poke that FAILS within a bar or two and a close beyond the line are opposite trades, and the micro line's strength-1 short-span pivots are a different object from the swing line even though the code is shared. Brooks's window is '2 to about 10 bars'; R00-39 read 6, T16-08 read 10, default 10.

ready.description: The bar overshoots the projected trend CHANNEL line -- the parallel of the trend line dragged to the far side of the price action -- by at least overshootAtr and closes back inside the channel: the fade of an overshoot, which Brooks treats as a sufficient reason to enter on its own.
ready.pseudocode: p1b, p2b = the bull trend line's two anchor bars; slope = (low[p2b] - low[p1b]) / (p1b - p2b); aBar = bar of the highest high between p1b and p2b; chanLine(k) = high[aBar] + slope * (aBar - k); high[0] > chanLine(0) + overshootAtr * atr(atrLength) && close[0] < chanLine(0)

complexity.reason: the trend line plus a search for the extreme pivot between its anchors to place the parallel

ready.merge_notes: T14-03 is the channel-line construction (the parallel anchored at the extreme pivot between the trend line's own two anchors, chosen so the bars in between are contained); R26-05 (stray, absorbed) is the only candidate here that states a trade on it -- an overshoot plus a good reversal bar is by itself enough reason to fade. The reversal-bar half is left to bar_anatomy_reversal_signal and ANDed in the pane; the overshoot half is this rule. T14-03's note that a channel line may instead be drawn through its own two pivots on that side is the alternative construction, recorded in design_decisions. This is also the measurable form of the climax bucket's V00-58 ('most climaxes end with trend channel overshoots').

ready.description: The first close through the trend line drawn from the first two swing pivots since the session open -- Brooks's 'first pullback to break a trend line', which he rates as one of the best entries because a second leg usually follows.
ready.pseudocode: sessionTrendDirection != 0 && !trendLineBrokenYetThisSession && close[0] > bearTlValueAt(0); set trendLineBrokenYetThisSession = true

complexity.reason: the trend line plus a once-per-session latch reset on the date change

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from TrendLineBreak because the 'first this session' latch changes which bars fire, not just how many. Intraday-only, tagged per the standing convention rather than dropped. Brooks warns (p409) that tiny pullbacks not breaking a meaningful line do not count as the first pullback -- swingStrength is the knob for that.

ready.description: Both of the last two legs are at least minLegBars bars long: the gap between the last two confirmed swing pivots and the bars since the most recent one both reach the minimum. Brooks's credibility test for the leg that breaks the trend line and the leg that tests the extreme.
ready.pseudocode: p1b = swingLowBar(swingStrength, 2); p2b = swingLowBar(swingStrength, 1); (p1b - p2b) >= minLegBars && p2b >= minLegBars

complexity.reason: bar counts only, but they come off confirmed swing pivots

ready.merge_notes: The only candidate in this bucket that is about leg SIZE rather than the line; kept here rather than pushed to leg_counting because it is stated as the qualifier on the trend-line-break leg and the test leg. Note for the roll-up: it measures legs by swing pivots, not by the decided HighLowBarCount counter (R17-01), so leg_counting may hold a behaviourally different rule with the same intent. Brooks allows an exception when one leg is one or two exceptionally large bars; not mechanized.

ready.description: A named Brooks setup: bars 2 and 0 form a two-bar reversal (skipping bar 1), and the skipped middle bar is small relative to recent bars. Enter beyond the combined extreme of the three bars.
ready.pseudocode: TwoBarReversal(bar2, bar0) && (high[1] - low[1]) <= middleBarMaxFraction * avgRange(rangeLookback); entry: buy stop one tick above the highest high of bars {2,1,0}

complexity.reason: reuses TwoBarReversal's ratios plus a small-middle-bar test; depends on TwoBarReversal (T06-05) being authored first

ready.merge_notes: T06-08 defines the three-bar shape (bars 2 and 0 form T06-05's two-bar reversal, skipping a small bar 1); T06-09 is its Entry order-type wrapper (stop above the three-bar combined extreme). T06-09 also describes an earlier-entry alternative when the last two bars alone already qualify as a two-bar reversal -- not mechanized here, just the standard stop-beyond-extreme entry (standing convention). Kept whole as a named Brooks setup, not split, per the composite-carrying rule for named setups (Harris-pattern precedent in the catalog).

ready.description: The close is within K ATRs of ANY of the mechanized levels -- the N-bar extreme above or below, the nearest round number, or the EMA. Identical both sides. Brooks's meta-filter: a reversal signal at a level is worth more than the same signal in open space.
ready.pseudocode: tol = magnetToleranceAtr * atr(atrLookback)[0]; absValue(close[0] - highest(high, lookback)[1]) <= tol || absValue(close[0] - lowest(low, lookback)[1]) <= tol || absValue(close[0] - (round(close[0] / roundStep) * roundStep)) <= tol || absValue(close[0] - ema(close, emaLength)[0]) <= tol

complexity.reason: an OR over four level constructions, one of which needs an EMA; each term is simple on its own

catalog_match.note: Not the same subject, but the same structural argument: DayOfWeekAnyOf exists precisely because entry panes AND, so an OR of alternatives cannot be composed from separate placements. This rule earns its keep for the same reason.

ready.merge_notes: Deliberately carried as a composite despite 'atomic beats composite', because the pane system ANDs entries: RoundNumberProximity AND TouchOfRecentExtreme AND EmaTouch requires ALL of them to be true, which is not what Brooks means. He means any one of them. That OR is unreachable from the parts, so it is a rule. All three sources say the same thing at different levels of generality -- R06-14 ('the closer the market gets to any magnet, the more likely it reaches it'), V19-11 (a named list: EMA, trend lines, channel lines, swing highs and lows especially yesterday's, breakout areas, range boundaries, measured-move targets), R09-05 (only trust a reversal at a key technical level). The level SET is narrowed to the four that are mechanized in this corpus today; trend lines, channel lines and measured-move targets are named by V19-11 but each needs its own bucket's primitive first, and each can be added as another OR term later. Tolerance in ATRs, from R09-05, rather than in ticks -- an OR across heterogeneous levels needs one scale-free band.

ready.description: Count how many of the last lookback bars touched the same support/resistance level within a tolerance. A low count means the level is still fresh; once the count reaches minTouches Brooks reads the level either as proven (repeated holds) or as worn out (each test consumes the orders defending it) -- the same measurement, used to favour a bounce or a breakout.
ready.pseudocode: touchCount = count over k in 1..lookback of (low[k] <= level + tolAtr * atr[k] && close[k] > level - breakTolAtr * atr[k]); touchCount >= minTouches

complexity.reason: needs a level to count against; the count itself is a window scan

ready.merge_notes: RP2-07 (touches weaken the level, favour the breakout) and T25-08 (touches that hold strengthen it) are the same touch counter read with opposite sign, so one rule with a per-placement direction. RP2-07 gives touchesForWeakening, T25-08 gives minTouches; default 3 sits between them.

ready.description: The most recently confirmed swing low is above the swing low before it (a higher low); mirror: the most recent swing high is below the one before it (a lower high). Brooks's minimum precondition for taking a with-trend trade: 'a trader usually should not be looking to buy unless the market is at least forming a higher low'.
ready.pseudocode: lastSwingLow(strength) > priorSwingLow(strength)

complexity.reason: needs the last two confirmed same-side pivots retained across bars

catalog_match.note: same shape at pivots rather than adjacent bars, and on the opposite series

ready.merge_notes: R00-30, V00-12 and TP3-07 are the same test. R02-25 ('the resumption stalls and forms a lower high with a bear signal bar') is this rule's SHORT side ANDed with a bear signal bar; atomic beats composite, so the signal-bar conjunct is left to bar_anatomy_reversal_signal and only the lower-high half is merged here. TP3-07 offers a cheap window proxy, lowest(low, n)[0] > lowest(low, n)[n] with n the leg length, which the authoring pass can use if pivot retention proves expensive.

ready.description: A test of support that holds: the bar's low comes within toleranceAtr x ATR of the most recent confirmed swing low WITHOUT trading below it (mirror: the high tests the last swing high from below without exceeding it). Brooks's 'test' - the market returns to a prior swing level and fails to break it.
ready.pseudocode: lastSwingLow(strength) <= low[0] && low[0] <= lastSwingLow(strength) + toleranceAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: needs the retained pivot price plus an ATR

ready.merge_notes: T03-04 states the general 'test' as a symmetric tolerance BAND around the pivot (2 ticks either side); T10-22 states the one-sided form, the low approaches but does not break the pivot, plus a close-up conjunct left to bar_anatomy. WINNER: the one-sided form - the two-sided band double-counts SwingPointUndercut, which already covers the break. Tolerance expressed as an ATR fraction (T10-22's 0.25) rather than T03-04's ticks so it ports across symbols; see the level-tolerance design decision. Kept apart from SwingPointUndercut (breaks the level) and DoubleExtreme (matches a level formed by a pivot, not necessarily the most recent one).

ready.description: Price has held beyond the prior swing high for at least barsBeyond consecutive bars without a pullback (mirror: below the prior swing low) - Brooks's stand-down rule: once the 'test' of the old extreme runs five or more bars past it, it is a successful breakout, not a reversal setup, and the countertrend trade is off.
ready.pseudocode: barsSince(low[0] < priorSwingHigh(strength)) >= barsBeyond

complexity.reason: a persisting bar counter over a retained pivot level

ready.merge_notes: Single source. Stated as a blocker for a countertrend entry, so in the pane system it is used negated; kept in its positive form since the negate toggle is per placement. V03-07's own trend-line-break gate belongs to lines_channels_trendlines and is ANDed there.

ready.description: The bar count from the three-push pattern's first push to the current bar lies inside [minBars, maxBars] — the book's size test that separates a wedge FLAG (10-20 bars) from a wedge REVERSAL (20+ bars) and from a micro wedge (<= 5).
ready.pseudocode:
patternBars = currentBarIndex - barIndexOf(swingLow(pushCount, swingStrength));
inWindow = patternBars >= minBars && (maxBars == 0 || patternBars <= maxBars)

complexity.reason: the count itself is trivial cross-bar state, but the start bar is the pattern's first pivot, so it inherits ThreePushPattern's pivot detection

ready.merge_notes: One rule with three book parameterizations, not three rules: wedge flag 10-20 bars (R18-04 = V05-07, the default), reversal-strength 20+ bars (R18-05 = V05-06, maxBars 0 = unbounded), three-legged pullback 5-15 bars (R11-12). R18-05/V05-06 also demand 'a clear trend channel line'; that half has no numeric definition anywhere in the bucket and is left to the trend-channel-line fit rule in lines_channels_channels — recorded here, not encoded.

ready.description: The three-push pattern has completed and the current bar reverses out of it: the close is beyond the prior bar's opposite extreme (long: close above high[1] after three pushes down). Signal-bar close then next-bar open, per the standing convention.
ready.pseudocode: isThreePushPattern[1] && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: the trigger is one comparison; the precondition inherits ThreePushPattern's pivots

ready.merge_notes: R18-02 and V05-04 (the with-trend 'wedge pullback, first signal' entry) and T03-10/V24-08 (the countertrend 'wedge reversal' entry) fire on the SAME bars — the with-trend/countertrend split is context supplied by other panes, not a different trigger — so they are one rule. V02-38 (stray, absorbed) is the same close > high[1] trigger with Brooks noting the signal bar may even be a bear trend bar, i.e. no signal-bar quality gate: that is what this rule already does, and any body/tail gate belongs to a separate bar_anatomy pane. V24-08's 'marginal new extreme within 6 ticks' maps to ThreePushPattern's maxPushExtensionTicks. T03-10's close>open term is dropped: close > high[1] already implies a strong up bar in the cases Brooks draws, and the body test is its own rule.

ready.description: After a three-push move, price closes beyond the pattern's most recent OPPOSITE pivot — the break of the wedge's other side (short when three pushes up are followed by a close below the most recent swing low).
ready.pseudocode:
// long side: three pushes DOWN, then close above the most recent swing high
isThreePushPattern[0] && close[0] > swingHigh(1, swingStrength)

complexity.reason: pivot detection for both the pattern and the level being broken

ready.merge_notes: Kept apart from ThreePushReversalEntry: a break of a pivot LEVEL and a close beyond the PRIOR BAR's extreme are different bars, often many bars apart. This is the order type V00-62 describes ('one tick beyond the breakout of the third push's opposite trend line'), mechanized as the pivot rather than a projected line.

ready.description: Compares the second push-to-push increment against the first: the pattern is accelerating (parabolic) when the later increment is the larger, decelerating ('shrinking stairs', waning momentum) when it is the smaller. One rule; the shrinking-stairs form is this one negated.

complexity.reason: needs three same-side pivots and their bar indices to difference and divide

ready.merge_notes: V05-08 (parabolic wedge: the later trend-channel-line slope steeper than the earlier one) and V05-09 (shrinking stairs: each breakout increment smaller than the last) are the same measurement with opposite senses, and the pane system's per-placement negate toggle covers the flip — so one rule, not two. They differ only in whether the increment is divided by the bar distance; that is the perBar input (1 = V05-08's slope, 0 = V05-09's raw price increments). V05-08's '2 legs / 10 bars' reversal expectation is guidance, not a condition, and is not encoded.

ready.description: The three-push pattern's own slope sets the expected breakout direction independently of the larger trend: a down-sloping wedge/channel is a bull-flag context (favor the upside break), an up-sloping one a bear-flag context.
ready.pseudocode:
// long side: the line through the pattern's pushes slopes DOWN
slope(swingLow(3, s), swingLow(1, s)) < 0

complexity.reason: a slope between two pivots, so it inherits pivot detection; the comparison itself is one sign test

ready.merge_notes: R18-09 ('an up-sloping wedge is a bear flag whether it is a pullback in a bear trend or a top in a bull trend') and R23-08 ('every bear channel, converging or not, functions like a bull flag') state the same test with different emphasis; R23-08 was graded research only because it OVERRIDES the engine's trend context, which is not a problem for a pane filter — as a pane it is just the slope sign. Graded B, not C, for that reason.

ready.description: After a three-push pattern, price comes back to within a tolerance of the pattern's own extreme without exceeding it, and the bar reverses away — fade the retest (short the test of a wedge high, buy the test of a wedge low).
ready.pseudocode:
// short side: a test of the wedge high
isThreePushPattern[k] && high[1] <= wedgeHigh && high[1] >= wedgeHigh - tolAtr * atr(atrLookback) && close[0] < low[1]

complexity.reason: pivot detection to fix the pattern extreme, plus an ATR-scaled retest band

ready.merge_notes: T21-78 (stray, absorbed) gives the mechanizable form — a double-top test of the wedge high within tolAtr, then a close beyond the prior bar's extreme — and R03-05 gives the same trade in words ('a buy signal at a third-push wedge high is a short'). R03-05's tolerance was 2 ticks; T21-78's 0.1 ATR is kept as the instrument-independent default. The general double-top/bottom machinery lives in swing_structure; this rule is the version anchored on the three-push extreme.

ready.description: The reversal out of a three-push pattern fails — price closes back beyond the pattern's extreme — so the pattern becomes a continuation: trade with the original channel direction instead.
ready.pseudocode:
// a wedge BOTTOM whose bull reversal failed: close back below the pattern low
isThreePushPattern[k] && reversalSignalFired[k] && k <= failureWindowBars && close[0] < patternExtremeLow

complexity.reason: pivots for the pattern plus persistent state for the reversal attempt and its failure level

ready.merge_notes: V05-17 ('if the breakout is weak, trade with the wedge channel instead — short the low 1 or low 2 the failed breakout creates'), T19-18 ('failed wedges and other failed reversals occur — a sign of trend strength') and V06-04 ('a failed expanding-triangle reversal makes it an expanding-triangle bull flag') are one behaviour on one pattern family. The mechanizable test is price closing back beyond the pattern's extreme within a window; V05-17's undefined 'weak breakout score' is dropped in favour of that. The low1/low2 counting that V05-17 mentions is HighLowBarCount (swing_structure), a separate pane.

ready.description: After a three-push/wedge extreme, the correction is treated as complete only once it has run at least a fraction of the pattern's own bar count.

complexity.reason: needs the pattern's first-push and extreme bar indices, so it inherits pivot detection; the ratio itself is arithmetic

ready.merge_notes: One rule, two book fractions: 'at least about half as many bars as the wedge' (R17-15, default) and 'at least a third or so' (T24-09). R17-15 also asks for 'two clear legs' in the correction — that is the HighLowBarCount leg counter (swing_structure), an AND-ed pane, not part of this test. T14-09 states only the two-legs half and was sent to leg_counting.

ready.description: The counter-based three-push entry: buy when the high/low bar counter just advanced to 3 (a High 3 / Low 3), which Brooks says trades identically to a wedge or triangle.
ready.pseudocode: highLowBarCount[0] == 3 && highLowBarCount[1] == 2

complexity.reason: one comparison on the persistent HighLowBarCount counter; no pivot search

ready.merge_notes: Kept SEPARATE from ThreePushPattern deliberately, though Brooks calls them functionally the same ('high 3 and low 3 patterns should be traded like wedges'): the counter fires on the bar that advances the count, the pivot detector fires once three confirmed pivots exist, and those are different bars. This is the cheap mechanization (the standing decision fixes the leg definition as R17-01's HighLowBarCount counter), so it should be authored and measured BEFORE the pivot-based pattern. V00-54 extends the same counter to 4 (High 4) — the same rule at count 4, recorded as a parameterization rather than a second rule.

ready.description: Named Brooks setup: after a trend has run for many bars, a mostly-horizontal pause showing two-sided trading — a high fraction of bars overlapping the prior bar by at least half — is a final-flag candidate.
ready.pseudocode:
overlapFrac = countIf(i in 0..flagBars-1, overlap(i) >= overlapThreshold) / flagBars;
isFinalFlagCandidate = trendDurationBars >= minTrendBars && overlapFrac >= minOverlapFraction

complexity.reason: a window loop over bar overlaps (easy) gated on a trend-duration counter built on AlwaysInDirection (persistent state)

ready.merge_notes: V07-01 wins the definition: it is the only source that reduces 'final flag' to something prospective (bar overlap fraction after an extended trend) instead of the retrospective label VP1-32 correctly calls circular. Its research grade came from the trend-duration term, which the standing always-in decision (AlwaysInDirection, two consecutive strong trend bars) now settles, so B not C. T03-11 contributes the flag's own minimum length (6 bars) and V07-06 the opposite extreme (a one- or two-bar pause after a StrongTrendBarRun spike still counts); flagBars 8 sits inside the book's usual 5-10. V07-06's 10-20 bar retest expectation is guidance, not a condition. The overlap test is deliberately NOT merged with HorizontalFlagWidthTest's range/ATR test — see that rule.

ready.description: Price closes through the COUNTERTREND side of a final-flag range — the last flag of the trend gives way the wrong way — optionally only after a with-trend breakout out of that flag has already been made and failed.

complexity.reason: Highest/Lowest windows are cheap; the precondition carries FinalFlagCandidate's trend-duration state

ready.merge_notes: All three are 'the flag's far side gives way'. V24-09 takes the break directly; R03-10 and R10-11 insist the market first breaks out WITH the trend, fails, comes back through the flag and out the other side — the same trigger with a precondition, carried as the requirePriorBreakout input rather than as a second rule. R03-10's barbwire framing is just a short flagBars.

ready.description: A final-flag reversal triggered and then failed within a couple of bars — price closes back through the reversal signal bar's own extreme — so the original trend resumes: a breakout-pullback entry with the trend.
ready.pseudocode: reversalFired[k] && k <= failureWindowBars && close[0] > high[k]

complexity.reason: carries FinalFlagCandidate's state plus persistent state for the failed reversal signal bar

ready.merge_notes: The final-flag twin of FailedThreePushReversalContinuation; kept separate because the precondition is a different pattern, so different bars. Both are listed on each other as near-misses for the authoring pass.

ready.description: The current always-in direction has held for at least N bars — the 'late in the trend' / 'the trend has gone on for dozens of bars' gate.
ready.pseudocode: barsSinceAlwaysInFlip >= minTrendBars

complexity.reason: a persistent counter reset by AlwaysInDirection flips

ready.merge_notes: R23-10 ('a triangle late in a trend tends to be the final flag', 30 bars) and V07-09 ('if the trend ran 50 to 100 bars the reversal becomes a large flag, not an opposite trend', 50 bars — a stray, absorbed) are one counter at two thresholds; 30 is the default, 50 recorded. Both sources spend their remaining content on what to EXPECT after the pattern, which is not a condition. Now B rather than C because the standing decision fixes always-in as AlwaysInDirection (two consecutive strong trend bars).

ready.description: Take profit at a prior swing pivot: the Nth most recent pivot on the chosen side becomes the target for the open position.

complexity.reason: the target level is a confirmed pivot, so the exit carries pivot detection

catalog_match.note: the catalog's targets are all dollar- or ATR-based (TakeProfit, AtrProfitTarget); none uses a structural level

ready.merge_notes: R05-21 targets the top of the wedge's SECOND push (pivotIndex 2) and V06-02 the expanding triangle's most recent opposing pivot (pivotIndex 1) — the same exit at different pivot indices, so one rule with an index input. R05-21's further 'and then the bottom of the wedge' is the same rule at a deeper index. Measured-move (pattern-height) targets are a different mechanism and went to exits_targets with TP2-06 and R23-04.

ready.description: Close the with-trend position once the third push has completed and the current bar turns against it — a channel usually pulls back after a third push.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && isThreePushPattern(UP)[0] && close[0] < low[1]

complexity.reason: pivot detection for the push count; the turn-down test is one comparison

ready.merge_notes: Stray, absorbed: the exit side of R02-37's observation that channels correct after a third push. Same pattern as ThreePushReversalEntry's precondition but in the exit pane, where an Entry rule cannot sit.

ready.description: Primitive: the first openingBars bars of the intraday session fix the opening-range high, low and height. As a filter the rule is true once the session is at least openingBars bars old, i.e. once the opening range is set. Every other opening-range rule in the corpus reads orHigh / orLow / orHeight from this one place.

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection off the Date series plus per-session persistent high/low/counter state; the definition itself is unambiguous

catalog_match.note: the corpus has no session-relative aggregate of any kind

ready.merge_notes: Four restatements, three of them (T22-01, T23-01, T24-01) literally the same pseudocode block copied per chapter, and each of those bundles the average-daily-range aggregate into the same block; that half is carried by AverageDailyRange and cited there rather than duplicated. TP4-01's statement is the cleanest: opening range = highest high minus lowest low of the session's first N bars. Book values for N: 'first five to 10 bars' (T21-63, V18-02), 'first 30 to 60 minutes' = 12 five-minute bars (TP4-01), 'first hour or two' = 24 bars (TP4-04, T22-01, T23-01, T24-01). Default 12, to be optimized. The bar-count form beats the clock form (Brooks's own '30 to 60 minutes') because it survives a change of bar interval and needs no session-open time input.

ready.description: Primitive: the mean full-session high-low range of the last dayLookback COMPLETED sessions, accumulated from the intraday series and rolled at each Date change. True once dayLookback completed sessions are in the ring.

complexity.reason: per-session high/low plus a ring buffer of completed session ranges; not a plain windowed average over bars

catalog_match.note: the corpus's volatility measures are all rolling N-BAR ATRs; this is a rolling N-SESSION range, a different window and a different quantity. On a daily series it degenerates to Average(High - Low, dayLookback) and needs none of the session machinery, which is why it is daily-ok.

ready.merge_notes: Two explicit statements of the primitive; T22-01, T23-01 and T24-01 define the identical aggregate inside their opening-range blocks and are merged into SessionOpeningRange, and R29-08's stop reads it. Book values: 'recent days' with no count (TP4-02, read as 5), 20 sessions (T22-01/T23-01/T24-01/T25-01). Default 20. Deliberately NOT the same as an ATR of daily bars: this averages high-low only, with no gap term, which is what Brooks means by 'the range of recent days'.

ready.description: The session's opening-range height, as a fraction of the recent average daily range, lies between lowFraction and highFraction. Under about 0.3 the day is 'in breakout mode'; a third to a half favours a trending trading range day; above about a half the opening move was a spike and the day is likely spike-and-channel.
ready.pseudocode: orSet && adrReady && orHeight >= lowFraction * adr && orHeight <= highFraction * adr

complexity.reason: one comparison pair once SessionOpeningRange and AverageDailyRange are available; all the machinery is in those two

ready.merge_notes: The single most-restated idea in the bucket: eight candidates measuring the opening range against the average daily range and reading a day type off the ratio. Book thresholds: 'about 25 percent' (V19-08, T23-01's quote), 'under 30 percent' (T21-63 explicitly, TP4-03, T23-02), 'a third to half' (TP4-04, T22-02), 'large' read as above 0.5-0.6 (V19-09, TP4-06). One rule with a low/high fraction band covers all four readings, and the 'large opening range' form is this rule with the band negated by the per-placement toggle (or with lowFraction raised), so it is not a second rule. TP4-06 adds a spike-DIRECTION term (close above the session open at the end of the opening range) and V19-09 adds a climactic-reversal caveat; both are separate concerns and are not carried here. T21-63, TP4-03 and V19-08 sit in the breakouts_other bucket and are cross-bucketed to here in this same pass, so they are merged once, here, where the two primitives they need are defined.

ready.description: The current bar is the first bar of the intraday session: its session date differs from the previous bar's. The structural gate under every opening-bar setup.
ready.pseudocode: ctx.Date(0) != ctx.Date(1)

complexity.reason: one comparison, but on the Date series rather than prices; needs the session model to agree with the data's session definition

catalog_match.note: CalendarBoundaryExit already reads Date(0) vs Date(1) (as year/month) and proves the Date series has real history, so no first-bar guard is needed; this is the same accessor testing the day change itself, on the Entry side

ready.merge_notes: Both are the same inferred structural helper, redefined per chapter exactly as the mining brief told the agents to. Neither is a Brooks statement; both are the definition every 'first bar of the day' rule needs. On a daily series this is true on every bar, so it is intraday-only by construction. SessionOpeningRange re-detects the same event internally; keep this one as the standalone gate for first-bar and second-bar setups (breakouts_other's SessionBarBreakout depends on it).

ready.description: The close sits near the midpoint of the session's range so far: |close - (sessionHigh + sessionLow)/2| <= f x (sessionHigh - sessionLow). Brooks's middle-of-the-day-middle-of-the-range caution, with the time half handled by TimeWindow.
ready.pseudocode:
mid = (sessionHigh + sessionLow) / 2;
absvalue(close[0] - mid) <= middleZoneFraction * (sessionHigh - sessionLow)

complexity.reason: needs the session's running high and low; the comparison itself is one line

catalog_match.note: CloseRangePosition places the close inside its OWN bar's range; this places it inside the SESSION's running range - same shape, different window, and this one is a middle-zone test rather than an upper/lower test

ready.merge_notes: RP4-17 is a composite of the middle-third-of-the-day window and this midpoint test. The window half is the TimeWindow duplicate (830..1030 in the book), so only the price half is carried here as an atomic rule; the pane system ANDs entries, so the book's filter is TimeWindow + this. Brooks himself flags the clock half as a guideline, not a rule ('the overriding factor is the price action'), which is another reason to keep the price half standalone.

ready.description: Protective stop sized as a multiple of the average bar range SO FAR TODAY (a session-relative, growing window), rather than a fixed dollar amount or a rolling N-bar ATR.

complexity.reason: a session-reset running sum and bar count; the exit test itself is the standard open-loss comparison

catalog_match.note: same 'size the stop by recent volatility' idea, but the window is 'since this session opened' and grows through the day instead of a fixed rolling N bars, and this is a fixed protective stop rather than a trailing one. Closest fixed-stop sibling is StopLoss with a volatility-sized distance, which the corpus does not yet have.

ready.merge_notes: Brooks quotes it as 'around the height of an average bar so far today, maybe 10 to 15 cents' - the dollar figures are stock-specific, the multiple is the portable form. Note the mining record's AvgTrueRange in el_words_needed is misleading: this is a mean of high-low, not of true range, and it is not the WFSafe_AvgTrueRange rolling accumulator.

ready.description: Protective stop sized as a fraction of the average daily range: Brooks's '50 to 75 percent of the average daily range' threshold for deciding the trend is over.
ready.pseudocode:
stopDistance = adrFraction * adr;   /* adr from AverageDailyRange */
ctx.OpenPositionLoss() >= stopDistance * ctx.BigPointValue()

complexity.reason: one multiplication once AverageDailyRange exists

catalog_match.note: AtrProfitTarget/AtrTrailingStop scale by an N-BAR ATR; this scales by an N-SESSION range and is a fixed protective stop

ready.merge_notes: Mined as research grade only because 'average daily range' was undefined; the AverageDailyRange primitive in this same bucket settles it, so this drops to B. Book values 0.5 to 0.75; default 0.6. On a daily series both this and its input are trivial, hence daily-ok.

ready.description: Trend-from-the-open: a per-session flag set the first time a bar closes beyond the first bar's high (bull) or low (bear), and cleared if price later closes back through the opposite extreme of that first bar. While the flag is set, the day is treated as a trend-from-the-open day in that direction.

complexity.reason: a small per-session state machine anchored on the first bar; no pivots, no counters over price

ready.merge_notes: R00-47 and V00-64 are the same glossary entry quoted verbatim in two volumes ('a trend that begins at the first or one of the first bars of the day ... and the start of the trend remains as one of the extremes of the day'). Coding that literally needs a no-pullback bar counter, a session-extreme tracker and a persistence test (earlyBarsWindow 3, minPersistBars 20) - three pieces of machinery for one context flag. T23-03 is the same chapter's own mechanical proxy ('as soon as a bar moves above the high of the prior bar, the day is a trend from the open bull trend day, at least for that moment') and needs only the first bar's two prices plus a flag, so it wins. The strict form's extra content - the extreme going unchallenged for most of the day - is carried separately by SessionExtremeSetInOpeningWindow, which measures exactly that.

ready.description: The session's opening price still sits within nearThreshold of the session's running low (bull case) - Brooks's sign of strength, a day that opens on its low often closing on its high.
ready.pseudocode: sessionOpen - sessionLow <= nearThreshold * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs the session's opening price and its running low; one comparison

ready.merge_notes: Brooks states it in hindsight ('the open of the day was very close to the low of the day'); the mined form makes it real-time by comparing the session open with the low SO FAR, which is monotone - once broken it stays broken for the session, exactly the behaviour wanted. Threshold in ticks, instrument-specific. Distinct from TrendFromOpenFlag: that one needs a close beyond the first bar, this one only needs the open to remain the extreme.

ready.description: Past the opening window, the session's low (long side) was made inside that window and price has come back near it - the 'the high or low of the day usually forms in the first hour' context, used to treat the level as the probable low of the day.
ready.pseudocode: barsIntoSession > firstHourBars && sessionLowBarIndex < firstHourBars && close[0] <= sessionLow + nearAtr * WFSafe_AvgTrueRange(atrLength)

complexity.reason: session-reset high/low tracking plus the bar index at which the extreme was set

ready.merge_notes: This is the measurable half of the strict trend-from-the-open definition (R00-47/V00-64): the day's extreme was set early and is still the extreme. Kept separate from TrendFromOpenFlag because it fires on different bars - it needs price back NEAR the level after the opening window, while the flag only needs the first bar's extreme taken out. The proximity term reuses WFSafe_AvgTrueRange (the register token for plain AvgTrueRange).

ready.description: At the end of the opening window, the net move from the session open exceeded a volatility threshold - the session had a strong first-hour trend leg - and its direction is held for the rest of the session.

complexity.reason: per-session state written once at a fixed bar count

catalog_match.note: Momentum compares the close with the close N BARS ago; this compares it with the SESSION OPEN at a fixed point in the session and then latches the result

ready.merge_notes: The trend-resumption-day precondition: 'the day has a strong trend in the first hour or so and then enters a trading range'. Measures the size and direction of the opening leg, where TrendFromOpenFlag only measures whether the first bar's extreme was taken out and OpeningRangeVsAvgDailyRange only measures the opening range's width. Latching at exactly firstHourBars (rather than re-evaluating) is what makes it a day-type flag rather than a momentum test.

ready.description: Once the number of trades taken in the current session reaches a cap, block further entries for the rest of the session: 'look for only three to five reasonable trades a day'.

complexity.reason: a per-session counter reset at the date change, incremented on each new entry

catalog_match.note: the corpus's only Switch: same 'stop trading for the period' shape, but keyed on a trade COUNT within a session rather than equity within a calendar month. MonthlyProfitTarget also forces flat; Brooks's rule only blocks new entries, so the Switch semantics need choosing.

ready.merge_notes: Book value 'three to five'; default 5. Whether it also forces flat (as MonthlyProfitTarget does) or merely blocks entries is an authoring choice - Brooks means the latter. TotalTrades(1)/EntriesToday would be the cheaper EL accessors if they measure the way this needs.

ready.description: While holding a countertrend position, if a second with-trend counting-setup signal (e.g. a High2 while short in a bull trend) fires against it, permit exiting the countertrend position or reversing to the with-trend direction.
ready.pseudocode: isSecondAdverseWithTrendSignal = isHigh2Setup[0] && isBullTrend[0]; allowExitOrReverseToLong = ctx.MarketPosition() == -1 && isSecondAdverseWithTrendSignal

complexity.reason: reuses the H2/L2 counting-setup primitive and a position-state read; the MA-proximity emphasis in the book is a strengthening condition, not a hard requirement

catalog_match.note: Same family as catalog's FlatOrOpenLossExceeds -- an Entry that reads position state to permit a reversal -- but gated on a with-trend counting setup instead of an open-loss threshold.

ready.merge_notes: Reads as a scale-in caveat in the book ('exit or reverse on the second move against a countertrend scale-in') but the rule itself is a single-position permission-to-exit-or-reverse; does not require holding multiple units. Depends on the H2/L2 counting-setup primitive, expected key High2Setup per T10-23/T00-19.

ready.description: After a recent volume peak, the bar makes a lower low than the previous bar on volume well below that peak — Brooks's volume divergence, a pullback-long signal in a bear trend; mirrored for shorts.
ready.pseudocode: peakVolume = highest(volume, lookback)[1]; low[0] < low[1] && volume[0] < divergenceFraction * peakVolume

complexity.reason: a bounded Highest over the volume series stands in for remembering the climax bar; no persistent state

ready.merge_notes: Stray from swing_structure. Brooks's 'remember the huge-volume bar' is mechanized as highest(volume, lookback)[1], which needs no state; 'one or two lower lows on less volume' becomes a single lower-low bar. divergenceFraction 0.5 and lookback 5 are the miner's readings.

tick.description: Brooks's 'best bull reversal bar': the minimum reversal-bar test plus at least M of the open/tail/overlap quality sub-tests. An M-of-N score, not an AND.
tick.pseudocode: reversalBarMinimum[0] && countTrue(reversalBarOpenNearPriorClose[0], reversalBarTailFraction[0], reversalBarLowOverlap[0]) >= minQualitiesRequired

complexity.reason: an M-of-N count over otherwise trivial sub-tests; each sub-test is cheap but the scoring shape is new to the corpus

tick.merge_notes: Carried as a composite under the named-Brooks-setup exception: 'the best bull reversal bars have more than one of the following' is the book's own scoring statement, and an M-of-N count is not reachable by ANDing panes. Graded by its hardest part, which is the count itself. The source also folds in a follow-through-bar term; that is dropped with V00-34 as a look-ahead condition.

tick.description: Each of the last N bars is a bull trend bar AND barely overlaps the bar before it (each bar's low is no more than X ticks below the previous bar's low): a Brooks spike with little overlap.
tick.pseudocode: for k in 0..spikeBars-1: close[k] > open[k] && (close[k] - open[k]) >= bodyFraction * (high[k] - low[k]) && (k == spikeBars-1 || low[k] >= low[k+1] - maxOverlapTicks * tickSize)

complexity.reason: a fixed-length loop combining a per-bar classification with a bar-to-bar overlap test inside the run

tick.merge_notes: V19-03 is V19-02 with spikeBars fixed at 2 plus a first-hour session gate; merged as a fixed parameter, and the session gate is dropped (it is TimeWindow from the catalog, ANDed in a separate pane). Kept apart from ConsecutiveTrendBars because the pairwise overlap term applies between adjacent bars of the run and cannot be ANDed in from another pane. Brooks's spikeBars: 2 for a light always-in read, 3-4 for a trend-day read; default 3.

tick.description: A small-range bar that closes up and whose low is within X ticks of the lowest low of the last N bars (short: mirrored) - the small bar shows the sellers have stopped at that level.
tick.pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) <= smallFraction * atr(atrLookback) && low[0] <= lowest(low, extremeLookback)[1] + nearTicks * tickSize && close[0] > open[0]

complexity.reason: an ATR window and a Lowest window, plus a proximity test on the current bar

catalog_match.note: CloseNearPriorLow measures the CLOSE against the single previous bar's low plus an offset; this measures the LOW against the lowest low of a window. Different bars.

tick.merge_notes: Two of its three terms are carried elsewhere (BarRangeAboveAtrMultiple negated, TrendBarBody at bodyFraction 0), but the proximity-to-a-recent-extreme term is not carried anywhere in this bucket, so the setup is kept whole rather than dropped as a composition. Brooks's actual test is a visual comparison against 'a big bar'; the window low is the mechanizable reading.

tick.description: A price gap left behind by a breakout is a magnet: the market is drawn back to fill or retest the gap's near edge, which serves as a target for a position taken away from it.
tick.pseudocode: gapLevel = low[g] where low[g] > high[g + 1]; low[0] <= gapLevel + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the gap's boundary must persist from the bar where it formed

tick.merge_notes: Same level test in three books. R10-09 states the magnet tendency generally (a true bar gap or a moving-average gap bar); V01-13 states it as an intraday context filter on a tracked breakout/measuring gap, so the same rule in the Entry role; T22-08 uses it as the cover target for a fade, with the gap being the two or three trend bars that carried price between two trading ranges (a band rather than a single level, hence the tolerance). Recorded as an Exit because two of three sources use it as a target; the authoring pass can place the same condition as an Entry filter.

tick.description: A gap up is followed within a few bars by a gap down whose range does not overlap the first gap (an island top); enter or hold short on a retest of the island's bottom.
tick.pseudocode: gap1 at i: low[i] > high[i + 1]; gap2 at j (j < i, i - j <= maxIslandBars): high[j] < low[j + 1] && low[j + 1] > high[i]; islandBottom = high[j]; high[0] <= islandBottom + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: two remembered gap events plus a non-overlap test between them, persisting across the island's width

tick.merge_notes: Kept apart from GapLevelRetest: that needs one gap, this needs a matched pair with a non-overlap constraint, so it fires on a small subset of the same bars.

tick.description: The prior bar poked no more than X ticks above the highest high of the bars before it and this bar has closed back below that level — a failed marginal breakout, traded in the reversal direction.
tick.pseudocode: level = highest(high, lookback)[2]; high[1] > level && high[1] - level <= barelyTicks * (MinMove / PriceScale) && close[0] < level

complexity.reason: an EL Highest read at a two-bar offset, plus two comparisons; Max Bars Back must cover lookback + 2

catalog_match.note: No catalog rule tests a failed breakout.

tick.merge_notes: R02-26 ('breaks a resistance level by only a tick or so and then reverses down') and R02-27 ('barely breaks one level but pulls back before reaching the next one that is just a little higher') are one behaviour: the breakout bar cleared the nearest level by almost nothing and price is back under it. R02-27's second, higher level cannot be mechanized without a set of remembered pivots (see the resistance-level design decision) and adds nothing on a fixed-window level, since not reaching a higher level is implied by reversing back under the lower one. Level taken as Highest(High, N)[2] — the extreme of the bars BEFORE the poking bar. B rather than A: it is a three-way test across three bar offsets and the [2]-offset Highest is easy to get wrong, but the definition itself is unambiguous.

tick.description: After a session opening gap up, the next bar trades at least one tick below the gap bar's low, back into the gap — a fade signal; mirrored after a gap down.
tick.pseudocode: SessionOpeningGapBeyondPriorExtreme[1] && low[0] <= low[1] - reversalTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: one-tick offset test on top of the session-gap primitive

tick.merge_notes: Three statements of the same glossary definition. T00-11 and V00-17's fixed prior-bar form won over R00-25's 'low of the session's first bar', which would need the first bar remembered across the day. V00-17 arrived as a stray from bar_anatomy_reversal_signal.

tick.description: The book's named major-trend-reversal setup, kept whole because Brian would want to test it as Brooks states it: a strong trend-line break, then a failed test of the trend's extreme, then a strong reversal signal bar on that test.
tick.pseudocode: barsSince(TrendLineBreak) <= testWindow && ExtremeTestAfterTrendLineBreak[0] && StrongReversalBar(up)[0]

complexity.reason: graded by its hardest part, the trend-line break and projection

catalog_match.note: the mining files list a likely_existing_rule of MajorTrendReversal, but no such rule is in rules/CATALOG.md -- it does not exist yet

tick.merge_notes: One of the named Brooks setups MERGE.md keeps as a composite. V24-14 is the mechanizable statement and supplies the parameters; V03-06 is the chapter's four-part definition, whose items 1-3 are the same three parts. V03-06's item 4 ('the second reversal goes far enough for a consensus that the trend has reversed') is DROPPED, not parameterized: Brooks gives no number, the mining file flags it as out of scope for a bar-level test, and inventing a consensus threshold would put the whole setup at C for no gain. With item 4 gone every part is measurable and the rule grades B. Its parts live in lines_channels_trendlines (TrendLineBreak, ExtremeTestAfterTrendLineBreak) and bar_anatomy_reversal_signal (the signal bar).

tick.description: When the bar that produced the entry had a range smaller than K x ATR — a weak, slow break rather than a decisive one — cap the trade at a scalp target instead of holding for a swing.
tick.pseudocode:
entryBarRange = the high-low range of the bar at BarsSinceEntry bars back;
entryBarRange < minBreakAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback) && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= scalpTicks * tickSize * bigPointValue

complexity.reason: needs the entry bar's range carried forward through the trade, then an ATR comparison and a profit test

catalog_match.note: AtrProfitTarget always exits at K x ATR of profit; this exits at a FIXED tick target but only when the entry bar was small, so it is a conditional target, not a scaled one

tick.merge_notes: The candidate anchors on 'the trend-line break bar', which would need the line machinery; re-anchored on the ENTRY bar, which the engine already knows and which is the same bar in the setup Brooks describes. That substitution is what makes it authorable at all.

tick.description: Exit the long when the high reaches the range-height measured move -- the top of the prior N-bar range plus that range's own height (mirrored for the short). Brooks's standard trading-range target.
tick.pseudocode: rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback)[1]; rangeLow = lowest(low, rangeLookback)[1]; target = rangeHigh + (rangeHigh - rangeLow); high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the stateless rolling form is two window extremes; the book's form freezes the projection at the breakout bar, which would need a persistent variable

catalog_match.note: Both are computed targets, but AtrProfitTarget scales open profit by ATR and never looks at where the range was; this projects a price from the window's own height.

tick.merge_notes: The stateless rolling form is taken over the book's frozen-at-the-breakout form, on the merge brief's most-mechanizable rule; R08-13's own notes propose exactly that simplification. The rolling target drifts as the window rolls, which is the cost -- flagged for the authoring pass. Brooks's own caveat is that the exact distance is only approximate however it is measured.

tick.description: Each time a strong trend bar closes in the trade's direction, ratchet the protective stop up to just beyond that bar's near extreme; the level only ever moves toward the trade, never away from it.
tick.pseudocode: if (ctx.MarketPosition() > 0) { if (close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= strongBodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])) trailLevel = maxList(trailLevel, low[0] - stopOffsetTicks * tickSize); } exitLong = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= trailLevel

complexity.reason: a monotonic per-position stop level held in a persistent variable and reset on each new entry

catalog_match.note: TrailingStop trails a dollar amount below the position's PEAK PROFIT; this trails a price level pinned to the last strong bar's extreme, so it can sit far from the peak and does not move at all through a run of weak bars.

tick.merge_notes: Four statements of the same ratchet. V24-36 and T11-07 both write the max() ratchet explicitly and are the winning definition. VP1-29 phrases the first application as 'move to breakeven' because in its example the strong bar's low happened to sit at the entry price; behaviourally it is this rule, not BreakevenStop. R01-02 defines 'strong' by RANGE instead of body, (high - low) >= 1.2 x ATR(14), rather than by body fraction; the body-fraction test wins because it needs no ATR call site and matches the rest of the corpus, and R01-02's range test is recorded here as the alternative reading. T11-07 triggers the ratchet on an add-on signal bar; without pyramiding that reduces to 'the most recent with-trend signal bar', i.e. this rule.

tick.description: A bar-by-bar trail that does not arm until the trade has shown a minimum open profit: before that the wider initial stop stands, after it the stop follows the prior bar's extreme.
tick.pseudocode: if (ctx.MaxPositionProfit() >= armProfitDollars) armed = true; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && armed && close[0] <= low[1] - stopOffsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: a once-true per-position arming flag, or equivalently a MaxPositionProfit read, gating a fixed-lag comparison

catalog_match.note: Same construction as the catalog's profit-gated time stop (an exit that cannot be composed from two panes because exits are ORed), applied to the bar-by-bar trail instead of a bar count.

tick.merge_notes: R29-14 is stated as a GATE on other tightening rules ('do not tighten until about four ticks of profit'), which the pane system cannot express, since exits are ORed and one exit cannot condition another. Recast as a single armed-trail exit, which is the only mechanizable shape. Brooks's alternative arming trigger, 'or a reasonably strong bar in your direction', is dropped from the merged form: that arming is already what TrailStopBehindStrongBar does. Using MaxPositionProfit rather than a hand-rolled flag keeps it to one accessor.

tick.description: Hold the wide structural stop while the trend has not once closed on the wrong side of the moving average; only after the first such close does the bar-by-bar trail arm.
tick.pseudocode: if (close[0] < ema(close, emaLength)[0]) emaBroken = true; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && emaBroken && close[0] <= low[1] - stopOffsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs an EMA plus a once-true per-position flag

tick.merge_notes: Same recast as TrailArmedAfterProfitThreshold: the book states it as 'do not use a tight stop while there have been no closes below the moving average', a gate the pane system cannot express, so it is carried as an armed trail. Brooks scopes the scan to 'since the current leg began'; anchored here to 'since entry', which is the mechanizable choice and avoids the leg-definition dependency (leg = R17-01's HighLowBarCount counter per the standing decision). minBars = 10 from the source is dropped: it is an artifact of the chart example, not a stated condition.

tick.description: The headline Brooks trail: while long, keep the protective stop just below the most recent confirmed swing low, raising it each time a new swing low forms; mirrored above the most recent swing high while short.
tick.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= swingLow(pivotStrength) - trailOffsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection; the pivot is confirmed only pivotStrength bars after it forms

catalog_match.note: TrailingStop and AtrTrailingStop trail a dollar or ATR distance below the position's PEAK PROFIT; this trails a chart level. On a trend that pauses, the dollar trail tightens with every new high while the swing trail does not move until a new pivot confirms.

tick.merge_notes: The single biggest collapse in the bucket: nine candidates from all three volumes, every one of them 'raise the stop to below the most recent higher low'. Uses the swing_structure bucket's SwingHigh/SwingLow with a strength parameter, per the standing decision. Four sources (RP3-10, R29-05, T18-22, R00-54) add a trigger, 'only after the market makes a NEW HIGH', which is redundant: a fresh swing low only becomes the most recent one after a rally, so the trigger adds no bars and is dropped to avoid a Highest() call site. R05-16 ('move the stop just above the failed breakout-test bar's high') merges here because a failed test bar's extreme IS a strength-1 swing pivot; it is the same mechanism named for the context it appears in. VP1-06 notes the same primitive also sets the INITIAL stop beyond the swing that began the spike; that static use is InitialStopBeyondSwingAtEntry, kept separate. Offsets are one tick everywhere; pivot strength is stated only by RP3-10 and T15-47, both 2.

tick.description: Risk to the swing low that existed when the trade was taken and leave the stop there: the level is captured at entry and never moved, unlike the trailed form.
tick.pseudocode: if (ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0) swingAtEntry = swingLow(pivotStrength); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= swingAtEntry - stopTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: swing-pivot detection plus a per-position captured level; with the lowest(low, stopLookback) proxy it drops to moderate

tick.merge_notes: Brooks's stop for limit-order channel entries: 'risking to below the most recent swing low'. Kept apart from SwingPointTrailingStop because the level is frozen at entry — on a trend that runs, the trailed rule exits far higher, and on a trend that never makes a new pivot the two are identical. T15-47 itself offers the mechanizable proxy lowest(low, stopLookback) captured at entry, which avoids pivot detection entirely and should be tried first.

tick.description: Arm the swing trail only after the trade has both pulled back to the area of the signal bar and then gone on to a new extreme; before that sequence completes, the wider initial stop stands so normal pullbacks in a tight channel cannot trap the trade out.
tick.pseudocode: if (low[0] <= high[ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + 1] + signalBarAreaAtr * atr(atrLookback)) retested = true; if (retested && high[0] > runningTrendHigh) armed = true; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && armed && close[0] <= swingLow(pivotStrength) - trailOffsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: swing pivots, an ATR, and a two-stage per-position sequencing flag

tick.merge_notes: The armed-trail recast again (see TrailArmedAfterProfitThreshold): the book states a gate, and a gate is only expressible as one compound exit. The 'area of the signal bar high' is quantified as a fraction of ATR because Brooks gives no number; T23-11's own signalBarAreaAtr = 0.25 is kept. Same arming idea as MoveStopToBreakevenAfterRetestAndNewHigh (merged into BreakevenStopOnSecondEntryTest), which arms a BREAKEVEN stop off the same retest-then-new-high sequence; the two should be compared once authored.

tick.description: For a trade entered during a spike, put the protective stop beyond the start of the spike (the first bar of the run of strong trend bars) rather than beyond the signal or entry bar.
tick.pseudocode:
// spikeStart = the first bar of the current run of consecutive strong trend bars
ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && close[0] <= low[spikeStartOffset] - stopBufferTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs the spike's start bar carried across bars, which is the same run-of-strong-trend-bars state the always-in primitive keeps

tick.merge_notes: Ranges chapter 7 and trends chapter 21 give the same stop for the same setup ('one tick below the low of the spike'). Both leave the spike's start to a separate primitive; anchored here to the start of the current run of consecutive strong trend bars, which is exactly the state AlwaysInDirection already keeps under the standing always-in decision (two consecutive strong trend bars flip the direction), so no new design decision is raised. This stop is deliberately wider than StopBeyondSignalBar: the reference bar can be several bars before the entry.

tick.description: Trail the stop into the most recent micro measuring gap: a two-bar-apart gap where a bar's low sits above the high of the bar two before it, which Brooks reads as a sign of strength that should not be violated.
tick.pseudocode: if (low[0] > high[2]) gapLevel = low[0]; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && gapLevel > 0 && close[0] <= gapLevel - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the gap test is a two-bar comparison, but the most recent gap's level has to persist across bars

tick.merge_notes: The gap test itself, low[0] > high[2], is trivial; all the machinery is in holding the last gap level. The gap detection half is independently meaningful and may belong in breakouts as a MicroMeasuringGap entry filter; carried here whole because as a stop it is the level, not the bar, that matters.

tick.description: Let the first pullback to the entry price go, then exit at breakeven on the second one: after price has touched the entry price, moved away in the trade's favour, and come back again, the trade is done.
tick.pseudocode: if (ctx.BarsSinceEntry() == 0) { touched = false; movedAway = false; } if (touched && high[0] >= ctx.EntryPrice() + awayTicks * tickSize) movedAway = true; atEntry = low[0] <= ctx.EntryPrice(); exitLong = ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && atEntry && touched && movedAway; if (atEntry && !touched) touched = true

complexity.reason: a two-flag per-position state machine reset on each new entry

tick.merge_notes: V15-13 is a stray absorbed here; T18-24 is the same sequence stated from the other end ('once a pullback tested the entry price and the market then made a new high, move the stop to breakeven — they do not want it coming back a second time'). Both need touch, recovery, return. The two differ only in the recovery test: V15-13 uses entry + awayTicks, T18-24 uses a new N-bar high. The tick offset wins as the more mechanizable of the two (no Highest call site) and because it measures what Brooks is actually describing, distance from the stop. Distinct from BreakevenStop, which exits on the FIRST return to entry.

tick.description: The leg 1 = leg 2 (AB=CD) measured move: with A the start of the first leg, B its end and C the end of the pullback, the target is D = C + multiple x (B - A). Exit the long there.
tick.pseudocode: A = swingLow(pivotStrength)[2]; B = swingHigh(pivotStrength)[1]; C = swingLow(pivotStrength)[0]; target = C + multiple * (B - A); ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: three swing pivots (A, B, C) must be tracked; the arithmetic is trivial once they exist

tick.merge_notes: Distinct from PatternHeightMeasuredMoveTarget by anchor pair: the height is the PRIOR leg and the projection starts at the PULLBACK extreme, not at the breakout extreme, so the two land on different prices whenever the pullback is not shallow. R07-07 is the canonical statement and wins the definition. R07-08 (nested legs: treat A-to-D as the new leg 1) is the same rule one scale up -- a pivotStrength/lookback parameterization, not a new rule. R16-03 anchors C at a breakout retest low rather than a pivot low; V06-03/V06-05 use the pattern's last leg as A-B and chain the anchor off a previously reached target; T21-47 uses the spike as leg 1 and the channel start as C. All are the same C + (B - A). Brooks rejects the ABCD/AB=CD labelling (R07-07, T01-06) but uses the construction constantly. R07-07's 'thick area' midpoint restatement resolves to the same price and is not encoded separately.

tick.description: While a pullback trading range is still forming, re-estimate the target every bar as twice the range's rolling midpoint minus the start of the pullback -- the target moves with the range instead of being frozen at entry.
tick.pseudocode: mid = (highest(high, rangeBars)[0] + lowest(low, rangeBars)[0]) / 2; target = 2 * mid - legStartCapturedAtEntry; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: a rolling Highest/Lowest midpoint recomputed each bar plus one price frozen at entry

tick.merge_notes: Same arithmetic as GapMidpointMeasuredMoveTarget but the midpoint is re-estimated on every bar as Brooks instructs ('keep adjusting the line'), so the target is a moving level and the two fire on different bars. Kept apart on that behavioural difference alone.

tick.description: For a countertrend long taken after a trend-from-the-open sell-off reverses, the measured move up equal to the open-of-day-to-low-of-day distance, projected from the day's low -- which resolves exactly to the session's opening price. Exit the long when the high reaches the day's open.
tick.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= sessionOpen + offsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: one session-anchored price (the day's open) held across the session

tick.merge_notes: The candidate writes target = reversalLow + (sessionOpen - sessionLow) with the reversal low being the day's low, which collapses to the session open -- so the mechanized rule is far cheaper than the candidate's own pseudocode suggests. The passage's second form ('a measured move up equal to about the height of the entire initial leg down') is LegOneEqualsLegTwoTarget and is not re-encoded here.

tick.description: The moving average is the minimum target of a countertrend scalp: exit the long when the bar's high reaches the N-bar EMA.
tick.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= xaverage(close, emaLength)[0] - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs an EMA; the comparison is single-bar

catalog_match.note: CloseAboveAverage is an Entry on a simple N-bar average of close; this is an Exit on the bar's HIGH against an EMA, and an Entry cannot sit in the exit pane.

tick.merge_notes: Two statements of the same scalp target (Ranges ch6 gaps, Trends ch10 second entries). T10-15 wins on precision (high[0] against the EMA, position-gated). Both note the trap T10-15 records: written for a long entered below the EMA, so a long entered above it exits immediately -- a placement concern for the authoring pass, not a change to the condition.

tick.description: The current signal bar's entry price is at or above the first signal bar's (mirror: at or below) - Brooks's trap test on a second entry: 'if the second entry is letting you in at a better price than the first, be suspicious. Most good second entries are at the same price or worse.'
tick.pseudocode: high[0] >= high[firstSignalBarIndex] - toleranceTicks * tickSize   // firstSignalBarIndex from the SecondSignal scan

complexity.reason: reuses SecondSignal's scan and compares one retained price

tick.merge_notes: Single source, kept as its own rule rather than folded into SecondSignal because it is a separate, independently meaningful test and Brooks states it as an override ('good fill, bad trade'); a placement can want the second entry without the price gate. It cannot be authored before SecondSignal, since it reads the same scan's first-signal bar. Figure 10.1's bar 10 is the book's counter-example: one tick better than bar 9, and it failed.

tick.description: Exit a high-N long (low-N short) as soon as price trades back below the count's signal bar low (above its high) before the position has reached a scalper's profit. Brooks: 'if the market reverses and trades below the low of the pattern before reaching at least a scalper's profit, the high 2 buy has failed.'
tick.pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] < signalLow && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < scalpProfitTicks * tickSize * bigPointValue

complexity.reason: reads HighLowBarCount's retained signalLow plus open-profit state

catalog_match.note: a stop at a PATTERN price (the signal bar's low) gated on not yet having made a scalper's profit, not a fixed dollar loss

tick.merge_notes: Single source, and an Exit, so it cannot be reached by placing FailedCountReversal in the exit pane (an Entry cannot sit there - the catalog makes the same call for ConsecutiveCloseExit). Same event as FailedCountReversal, opposite use: that one takes the other side, this one just gets out. R17-12's own note is worth keeping: a failed count usually becomes the next count number, which is simply HighLowBarCount continuing to advance, so no separate rule is needed for 'a failed high 2 becomes a high 3'.

tick.description: The bar's high trades beyond the projected trend channel line (the parallel of the trend line on the far side of the channel) -- the bare penetration, with no reversal requirement.
