tick.pseudocode: high[0] > channelLine[0] + overshootTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection, the trend line through two same-side pivots, and its parallel through the extreme pivot between them

tick.merge_notes: R00-44 and V00-59 are the same one-line test, restated verbatim from the two glossaries. TP2-02 and T15-07 are the LINE CONSTRUCTION rather than a firing condition, kept here as citations because this is the first rule that uses it: the parallel of the trend line anchored at the extreme pivot lying between the trend line's two anchors, pivotStrength 2, identical in both books (T15-07 p269 adds that the anchor should be the swing that 'contained all of the sell-offs', which the highest high between the anchors satisfies). R00-43's 'micro trend channel line' fits a line across the highs of three to five consecutive bars instead -- the same object over a fixed window rather than pivots; recorded in design_decisions as the cheap alternative. Every rule below that names channelLine[0] uses this construction.

tick.description: The bar approaches the projected trend channel line to within a band but does not reach it -- the market reverses away without touching the line.
tick.pseudocode: high[0] < channelLine[0] - undershootTicks * tickSize && high[0] > channelLine[0] - undershootBandTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the channel-line projection, plus a two-sided band

tick.merge_notes: The two glossaries again. Not ChannelLineOvershoot negated: the negation would fire on every bar nowhere near the line, so the band's outer edge is the content. V00-60 gives 5 ticks, R00-45 gives 4; 5 chosen. Neither source states the 'and then reverses' half in any measurable form, so it is left out.

tick.description: After a bar closes beyond a channel's line, do not take that breakout; wait for the pullback that retests the channel's old extreme and enter on the signal bar that forms there.
tick.pseudocode: exists b in 2..maxPullbackBars with close[b] > channelLine[b] (breakout bar) && low[1] == lowest(low, b-1) (the pullback low) && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: the channel line, plus breakout and pullback state tracked over an open-ended window

catalog_match.note: The generic breakout-pullback primitive lives in breakouts_pullback_retest; this is that primitive gated on a channel breakout.

tick.merge_notes: Three statements of one setup at three scales: T21-29 after a spike-and-channel breaks, RP3-12 after a steep channel's trend-line break ('the test can be a lower high, a double top, or a higher high' -- so which retest shape qualifies is a parameter, not three rules), V24-21 after a micro channel breaks. V24-21's minChannelBars = 4 micro-channel gate is MicroChannelRunLength ANDed in, not part of this rule. The authoring pass should check this against the breakouts_pullback_retest bucket's generic breakout-pullback rule before authoring a second one.

tick.description: The close is beyond the projected trend line: for the long side, above the bear trend line drawn through the two most recent confirmed swing highs of the prior down move (mirrored: below the bull trend line drawn through the two most recent swing lows). Fires on the break bar itself.
tick.pseudocode: p1b = swingHighBar(swingStrength, 2); p2b = swingHighBar(swingStrength, 1); require high[p2b] < high[p1b]; bearTl0 = tlValue(high[p1b], p1b, high[p2b], p2b, 0); close[0] > bearTl0 + breakTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: two confirmed swing pivots plus a projected line value (TLValue); the line only exists once the second pivot is confirmed, swingStrength bars after it prints

catalog_match.note: nothing in the catalog projects a line through pivots

tick.merge_notes: Fourteen restatements of one test. The construction decision (see design_decisions 'trend-line construction') is: the two most recent CONFIRMED swing pivots on the trend side, priced at the pivot bar's high/low, projected with TLValue; if the second pivot is not beyond the first in the trend direction the line is undefined and the rule is false. TP2-01/T13-02/T14-02/T15-06 are the identical construction statements from four chapters (citations, not separate rules). 'Minor' vs 'major' is this rule at different parameters, not two rules: R11-13 minor = swingStrength 1 over ~15 bars, R11-18 major = swingStrength 3 over ~50 bars, T16-10 calls a line 'major' once it is ~12 bars old. V02-19's 'break by many ticks' is breakTicks = 8 on the same test (the mining file itself calls it a parameterization of V02-10). T13-12 (anchor on candle bodies, min(open,close), instead of tails) and T14-10 (redraw through the first two pullback lows instead of the trend-channel-line parallel) are construction ALTERNATIVES, recorded in design_decisions; both are strays absorbed here as citations. Break is close-based in every source that states one; a high/low-based break is the recorded alternative.

tick.description: After a bear trend line was broken to the upside, the pullback's lowest low stays at or above the projected old line and the bar closes up -- broken resistance acting as support (the breakout test of the line).
tick.pseudocode: lowest(low, pullbackBars) >= oldTlValue(0) - toleranceTicks * tickSize && close[0] > open[0]

complexity.reason: the broken line must keep being projected after the break, i.e. its anchor pivots are frozen at the break rather than following the newest pivots

tick.merge_notes: Kept apart from TrendLineTouch: that one tests an INTACT line from the trend side, this one tests a BROKEN line from the far side, and the two need opposite anchor-freezing behaviour (TrendLineTouch always uses the newest pivots; this one must keep the pre-break pair). The frozen-anchor requirement is the one place where the 'always redraw from the newest pivots' construction decision does not apply, and it is called out in design_decisions.

tick.description: A trend-line break happened within the last withinBars bars and price has now come back to within tolTicks of the trend extreme that stood at the time of the break -- the second half of Brooks's break-then-test reversal sequence.
tick.pseudocode: barsSince(TrendLineBreak) <= withinBars && abs(high[0] - extremeAtBreak) <= tolTicks * tickSize, where extremeAtBreak = highest(high, withinBars) as of the break bar

complexity.reason: needs the break event and the pre-break extreme both persisted; the current-bar test is one comparison

tick.merge_notes: Kept whole rather than split into TrendLineBrokenRecently AND a level test, because the level tested is the extreme AS IT STOOD AT THE BREAK, which no separate pane can reference. R04-03 is this same condition used NEGATED (block a with-trend breakout buy that is really a post-break retest) -- a per-placement toggle, so the same rule. T13-04 adds the line-age gate (matureBars, 'in effect for dozens of bars'), carried as a parameter. VP1-03 (stray, absorbed) is the cleanest statement of the level test and supplies tolTicks = 2; R00-51 supplies 4. Five further candidates state this AND a reversal-bar-quality term (V02-11, V13-02, T05-07, T17-06, plus the stray TP4-11); they are dropped as compositions since the reversal-bar half belongs to bar_anatomy_reversal_signal and the pane system ANDs entries.

tick.description: The close is within a tick tolerance of the classic floor-trader daily pivot, (priorDayHigh + priorDayLow + priorDayClose) / 3. Identical both sides.
tick.pseudocode: pivot = (priorSessionHigh + priorSessionLow + priorSessionClose) / 3; absValue(close[0] - pivot) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: on an intraday series it needs the prior session's high, low and close carried across the session boundary; on a daily series it is (high[1] + low[1] + close[1]) / 3, which is trivial

catalog_match.note: Both test proximity to a session-derived reference. CloseWithinAtrOfVwap tracks the CURRENT session's volume-weighted price and scales its band by ATR; this reads three fixed values from the COMPLETED prior session and uses a tick band.

tick.merge_notes: A stray sent here from swing_structure, and it fits: it is another constructed level in a file of constructed levels. Brooks writes only 'daily pivots' and names no formula, so the classic (H + L + C) / 3 is chosen -- the one everyone means by the bare phrase, and the only one of the three families (classic / Woodie / Camarilla) that needs no extra weighting choice. R1/S1 and the wider bands are deliberately not carried; add them as a ratio input if the base level tests out. On a daily (M1440) series this collapses to a prior-bar expression and is priority A work; it is graded B for the intraday case, which needs the session boundary.

tick.description: The opposite extreme of a recent notable bar -- a large trend bar, or the signal/entry bar of an earlier setup -- is remembered as a support/resistance level, because the protective stops of the traders who entered there rest just beyond it. The level persists until it is tested: price either turns at it (limit test) or probes a few ticks past it and closes back on the trend side (a stop run).
tick.pseudocode: level = low[k] where bar k is the most recent LargeTrendBar or long signal bar within recentBars; testHolds = low[0] <= level + testTicks * tickSize && close[0] > level; stopRun = low[0] < level - runTicks * tickSize && close[0] > level

complexity.reason: needs a persistent level recorded at a notable bar and held across bars until tested

catalog_match.note: no catalog rule remembers a level from an earlier bar

tick.merge_notes: R10-12 states the level primitive; R10-13 is the stop-run-then-reverse trigger on it; R28-14 is the resting limit a tick or two above the original spike signal-bar high, the same level used as a test. Merged as one rule because the level is the machinery and both triggers are one comparison against it.

tick.description: The bar's low trades at or below the most recent confirmed swing low, by at least offsetTicks (mirror: the high trades at or above the most recent swing high). Brooks's universal countertrend/limit trigger: 'buy at or below the low of a prior swing low', 'buy below a swing low expecting the breakout to fail'.
tick.pseudocode: low[0] <= lastSwingLow(strength) - offsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs the most recent confirmed pivot's price retained across bars; the comparison is trivial once it exists

tick.merge_notes: Eleven candidates, one behaviour. Seven are the plain limit trigger at the last swing point (R26-14, R28-21, T21-18, T21-22, R28-40, T18-20, R04-05 on the short side) differing only in the CONTEXT GATE they attach - trading-range bottom, bull channel, bear channel, pullback-inside-a-bull-trend, late-stage channel - every one of which is a rule in another bucket and is ANDed by the pane system, so none of them changes this condition. V03-03 ('the test overshoots the old extreme: low[0] < priorSwingLow') is the same test after a trend-line break. V03-04 and R05-20 are the NEGATION (low[0] > priorSwingLow, the test undershoots / the stairs structure holds), which is the per-placement negate toggle and therefore the same rule. R04-05 and R26-14 attach scale-in sizing (add at each successive swing high, half-size first leg) which the engine cannot express; recorded and dropped. R28-16 places the limit below BOTH the prior bar's low and the swing low - the extra conjunct is a one-bar test that belongs with bar-level pullback rules. Standing convention applies: the limit fill is mechanized as signal-bar close then next-bar open, so offsetTicks defaults to 0 rather than Brooks's 'one tick below'.

tick.description: The close is above the most recent confirmed swing high by at least marginTicks (mirror: below the most recent swing low). At swingPointsCleared > 1 the close must be beyond that many of the recent same-side pivots - Brooks's 'it reverses many bars, swing highs, and bear flags of the prior trend'.
tick.pseudocode: count of confirmed swing highs p within maxBarsBack with close[0] > swingHighPrice(p) + marginTicks * tickSize >= swingPointsCleared

complexity.reason: needs retained pivot prices; trivial arithmetic once they exist

catalog_match.note: the catalog rule uses a FIXED N-bar window, Highest(High,N)[1]; this uses the pivot, which is Brooks's stricter reading and fires at a different, structure-dependent level

tick.merge_notes: R00-35, VP1-23 and TP3-19 are identical at the defaults. V02-18 adds a margin ('breaks resistance by many ticks', 4) - a threshold, so a parameter. V02-05 requires the close to clear at least K swing highs of the prior trend (K = 2) - that is this rule at swingPointsCleared = K, and at K = 1 it degenerates to the others, so one rule. Every source flags that a fixed-window proxy exists and IS the catalog's CloseAbovePriorHighestHigh; the four candidates that state ONLY the proxy are collected separately as a D duplicate. Kept apart from that duplicate because the pivot level and the N-bar-highest level genuinely differ: after a deep pullback the last swing high can sit far below the N-bar high.

tick.description: Take profit when open profit is at least profitThreshold dollars AND price reaches the most recent confirmed swing high plus offsetTicks (mirror: the last swing low minus offsetTicks for a short); a negative offsetTicks takes profit just BELOW the old high, which is what Brooks does once the rally is weakening.
tick.pseudocode: ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= profitThreshold && high[0] >= lastSwingHigh(strength) + offsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs a retained pivot price; the profit test is trivial

catalog_match.note: TakeProfit is the dollar leg alone; exits are ORed, so a dollar target AND a price level cannot be composed from two exit rules and must be one rule

tick.merge_notes: T18-23 takes profit ABOVE the most recent swing high once profit is large enough; R30-06 takes it AT OR SLIGHTLY BELOW that high once the rally is judged to be maturing. One rule with a signed offsetTicks: +1 is T18-23, -3 is R30-06. R30-06's 'maturing/weakening trend' gate is research-grade with no bar-level test in that chapter and is dropped, which is what keeps this rule out of C; the profit threshold is a reasonable stand-in for 'the trend has run far enough'. Both describe PARTIAL profit taking, which the engine's whole-position Exit cannot express - recorded as a full-exit approximation, per T18-23's own note.

tick.description: The double bottom pullback: after a double bottom formed within the last patternWindow bars and price rallied away from it, a third push down holds ABOVE the double bottom's level, coming no closer than holdTicks and no further than testZoneAtr x ATR (mirror: the double top pullback). Brooks: 'a three-push bottom where the third push down did not have strong-enough sellers to create a new low' - one of his most reliable buy setups.
tick.pseudocode: doubleBottomLevel = level of DoubleExtreme fired within patternWindow; low[0] > doubleBottomLevel + holdTicks * tickSize && low[0] < doubleBottomLevel + testZoneAtr * atr(atrLength)

complexity.reason: inherits DoubleExtreme's retained pivots and adds a remembered pattern level plus a zone test

tick.merge_notes: Carried as a composite because it is a NAMED Brooks setup (the double bottom pullback / double top pullback) that Brian would want tested as the book states it, and because the third push's relationship to the pattern LEVEL is not expressible by ANDing DoubleExtreme with HigherSwingLow - the pane would not know the higher low has to sit just above the double bottom specifically. V08-02 gives the zone reading (hold margin 0, test zone 5 ticks), T07-47 the pivot-pair reading, V00-29 the loosest ('a double bottom followed by a deep pullback that forms a higher low'). Zone expressed in ATR for portability. V08-02's own note is important: Brooks treats the third push ending AT the level (a triple bottom) or slightly BELOW it and reversing (a failed breakout) as the same setup, so holdTicks should be allowed to go negative rather than the zone being widened. Graded by its hardest part, DoubleExtreme.

tick.description: The double bottom fails: after a double bottom formed within the last patternWindow bars, the low breaks breakTicks below its level (mirror: price breaks above a double top). Brooks: 'if a double bottom bull flag sets up but the market immediately reverses and falls below the double bottom, there might be a downside measured move' - traders enter on a stop one tick below.
tick.pseudocode: doubleBottomLevel = level of DoubleExtreme fired within patternWindow; low[0] < doubleBottomLevel - breakTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: inherits DoubleExtreme's retained pivots plus a remembered level and a failure window

tick.merge_notes: R12-05 is the pattern breaking in the direction of the break (the double bottom fails, sell below it), stated with a failure window of 3 bars. V05-13 is the OTHER failure - price breaks ABOVE the double top and then closes back below it within a few bars, which Brooks reads as the third push of a wedge top - and that shape is FailedBreakoutBeyondExtreme applied to the double-top level rather than to an N-bar extreme; it is merged here as a citation and listed in variants_kept_separate on both, because whether the entry is with the break or against it is the whole difference between the two trades. The note on this rule for the authoring pass: author the with-the-break form (R12-05) first; the against-the-break form composes DoubleExtreme with FailedBreakoutBeyondExtreme once that rule can take a supplied level.

tick.description: The book's literal double-top entry: after a double top, sell when price breaks entryTicks below the LOW OF THE DIP between the two tops (mirror: buy above the high of the bounce between the two bottoms of a double bottom).
tick.pseudocode: dipLow = lowest low between the two swing highs forming the double top; low[0] <= dipLow - entryTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: inherits DoubleExtreme's pivots and additionally needs the extreme BETWEEN the two pivots retained

tick.merge_notes: Single source, kept apart from DoubleExtremeBreakout because the level is different: this one triggers at the DIP between the two extremes (much further away) rather than at the pattern's own level. Worth authoring precisely because Brooks says it fails: 'that is rarely successful because 80 percent of breakouts fail' - which under the per-placement negate toggle is a testable claim in both directions. Needs the between-pivots extreme, which is one more piece of retained state than any other rule in this bucket.

tick.description: The market has made N successive swing extremes in one direction, each beyond the last, inside a lookback window: the generic three-push shape. Wedge, triangle, three pushes, micro wedge and head-and-shoulders are all this one detector at different parameters; the convergence/divergence of the connecting lines is a parameter (shapeMode), not a separate pattern.

complexity.reason: needs confirmed swing pivots (SwingHigh/SwingLow at a strength) plus a walk over the last three same-side pivots; the shape test adds two slopes

tick.merge_notes: Eleven restatements of one primitive across all three books. V05-01 wins the definition: Brooks says explicitly that wedge, micro wedge, parabolic wedge, triangle, expanding triangle, triple top/bottom and head and shoulders 'do not matter' — three pushes is the whole setup — so the shape test is a parameter (shapeMode) defaulting to OFF rather than a gate. R23-01's triangle ('three pushes one way, two the other') is the same bars: three same-side pivots imply two intervening opposite pivots. T14-08 supplies the only numeric convergence test in the bucket (trend-line slope > channel-line slope x 1.1) and becomes shapeMode 1's convergenceMultiple. V05-11's micro wedge is this rule at swingStrength 1 with ThreePushDurationWindow(1, 5). pushCount 3 is Brooks's stated minimum everywhere; swingStrength 2 is the mined default (T03-10 used 3). lookbackBars: 40 (R02-37, V24-08) vs 30 (R18-01); 40 kept. Push-count resets (a very large trend bar, an outside bar, an especially strong second push) are NOT in this rule — see PushCountResetOnStrongPush.

tick.description: Thin variant of ThreePushPattern: at least minLegs alternating pivots where BOTH sides diverge — each swing high above the swing high two pivots back and each swing low below the swing low two pivots back.

complexity.reason: same pivot machinery as ThreePushPattern, applied to both sides across five or more pivots

tick.merge_notes: Kept as a thin variant rather than a parameterization because the two-sided divergence test is not expressible as ThreePushPattern(shapeMode=2), which only looks at one side's pushes. V06-01's five-leg two-sided form is the definition; VP1-17 is the same with three pushes; V24-19's one-sided form (each push exceeds the prior by >= 4 ticks) is ThreePushPattern with minPushExtensionTicks = 4 and is recorded as that parameterization, not a separate detector. V06-06 ('a failed breakout grows it to seven then nine legs') is the same rule with minLegs as a lower bound, exactly as its own note concedes. The reversal entry off the pattern is ThreePushReversalEntry; the target is SwingPivotTarget.

tick.description: Three pushes in which each new extreme beats the prior one by only a tick or two, then price closes beyond the LAST push's extreme — a wedge that fails to reverse and instead breaks out with the pushes.
tick.pseudocode: isThreePushPattern[0] with maxPushExtensionTicks = 2 && close[0] > swingHigh(1, swingStrength)

complexity.reason: pivot detection plus a per-push extension cap in ticks

tick.merge_notes: Stray, absorbed. Behaviourally the opposite trade to ThreePushSwingBreakoutEntry (with the pushes, not against them), so kept separate despite sharing the primitive. The source's 3-to-20-bar pullback between the marginal breakouts is exactly what a confirmed pivot at swingStrength 2 already enforces, so it is not carried as a second parameter.

tick.description: Named Brooks setup: a three-push pattern whose MIDDLE push is the most extreme and whose two outer pushes are roughly equal — a head-and-shoulders top (mirrored for a bottom).
tick.pseudocode:
ls = swingHigh(3, s); head = swingHigh(2, s); rs = swingHigh(1, s);
isHeadAndShouldersTop = head > ls && head > rs && absValue(ls - rs) <= shoulderSymmetryTicks * tick

complexity.reason: ThreePushPattern's pivots with the ordering test changed from monotone to peaked, plus a symmetry tolerance

tick.merge_notes: Kept as a named composite (Brooks calls it a wedge whose third push fails to surpass the second) because Brian would want it tested as the book states it. It is NOT ThreePushPattern at a parameter: the monotone 'each push beyond the last' test is replaced by a peaked one, so different bars. R12-04's head-and-shoulders CONTINUATION variant is the same shape plus a double top/bottom around the right shoulder; the double-top half is swing_structure's rule, AND-ed as its own pane. The neckline is not in this rule — see HeadAndShouldersNecklineBreakout.

tick.description: The literal head-and-shoulders entry: price closes beyond the neckline, the line through the two pullback extremes between the shoulders and the head.
tick.pseudocode:
necklinePrice = lineValue(swingLow(3, s), swingLow(2, s), currentBarIndex);
isHeadAndShouldersTop[0] && close[0] < necklinePrice - entryTick * tick

complexity.reason: inherits the pattern's pivots and adds a two-point line projected to the current bar

tick.merge_notes: Kept because it is the textbook entry Brooks is arguing AGAINST ('a breakout below the neckline in a bull market will usually fail'), which makes it worth testing as stated — and testable negated, which is the trade he recommends.

tick.description: The high and low made in the premarket/overnight window are held as levels through the day session; the bar tests one of them within a tick tolerance. Brooks treats the premarket extremes as targets that usually get tested once the day session opens.
tick.pseudocode:
if (ctx.Time(0) > premarketStart && ctx.Time(0) <= premarketEnd) { pmHigh = MaxList(pmHigh, high[0]); pmLow = MinList(pmLow, low[0]) }  /* reset at the session date change */
ctx.Time(0) > premarketEnd && high[0] >= pmHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: segments each session's bars into a premarket window by clock time, accumulates an extreme over just that window, and holds it for the rest of the session

tick.merge_notes: Only one candidate, and the only rule in the bucket that needs a SECOND session window (premarket) beside the day session; it therefore rides on whatever session model the design decision settles. Requires the data feed to include Globex/overnight bars - on a regular-session-only series the rule can never fire. Same shape as PriorSessionLevelTest but the level comes from a within-day window rather than the previous session, so they are kept apart.

tick.description: The prior session closed strong - its close was near the high of its final closingWindowBars bars - which biases the next session bullish. A flag computed at one session's end and consulted through the next.
tick.pseudocode:
at the last bar of a session: closedStrong = close[0] >= highest(high, closingWindowBars) - toleranceTicks * tickSize;
during the next session: return closedStrong

complexity.reason: needs session-END detection (the bar before a date change is only knowable one bar late, or via a session-close clock time) and state carried across the boundary

catalog_match.note: same 'where did it close in the range' idea, but over the session's closing window and carried into the next session

tick.merge_notes: Brooks's point is about the daily bar's shape: a 5-minute rally into the close makes the daily bar a bull trend bar and biases the next bar. Note the mechanization trap: the last bar of a session is only identifiable one bar late (when Date changes) unless a session-close clock time is an input; the clock-time form is the cheaper one and matches the corpus's TimeWindow habit. closingWindowMinutes 45 in the book = 9 five-minute bars.

tick.description: After price briefly trades beyond a recent swing extreme against the trade direction but immediately closes back in the trend direction, enter (or re-enter) on a stop one tick beyond the prior bar's extreme.
tick.pseudocode: stopRunOccurred = low[1] < recentSwingExtreme && close[1] > recentSwingExtreme; enterLongNextOpen = stopRunOccurred && high[0] >= high[1] + entryTick

complexity.reason: needs a tracked recent swing-extreme/stop-cluster level and a breach-then-reclaim detector before the ordinary stop-entry mechanization

tick.merge_notes: Source frames this as 'add to or re-enter' a swing position (multi-unit language), but the mechanism itself -- a breach-and-reclaim of a recent level, entered on a stop -- does not require holding multiple units. Reduces to a single-position Entry (a stop-run continuation entry); mechanized that way, dropping the 'add to an already-open position' framing.

xaverage_lag.description: The first bear trend bar whose close falls below the moving average, after the previous bar closed at or above it: buy at the next open. Short is the mirror.
xaverage_lag.pseudocode: close[1] >= ema(close, emaLength)[1] && close[0] < open[0] && (open[0] - close[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && close[0] < ema(close, emaLength)[0]

complexity.reason: needs an EMA plus a two-bar crossing test and a bar classification

catalog_match.note: The EMA half belongs to ema_relations; nothing in the catalog crosses an EMA with a bar-colour requirement.

xaverage_lag.merge_notes: Kept whole because the long entry requires a BEAR trend bar: flipping a TrendBarBody placement to get that would also flip the EMA test to the wrong side. The 'strong bull trend' qualifier is left to an external context pane. The EMA half duplicates an ema_relations rule (first close below the moving average); flagged for that merge agent by way of this note - XAverage has no register row yet.

xaverage_lag.description: The second attempt at the moving-average-gap-bar fade: take the gap-bar breakout only when one earlier attempt has already failed, and never a third.
xaverage_lag.pseudocode: gapBarAttempts == 1 && high[1] < ema(close, emaLength)[1] && close[0] > high[1]

complexity.reason: needs a persistent attempt counter that increments on each failed fade and resets when the trend's extreme is tested

catalog_match.note: No catalog rule remembers whether an earlier signal failed.

xaverage_lag.merge_notes: Brooks's 'count to two, then stop' applied to the gap-bar fade, stated three times as the retry (R13-04, R14-03, R06-10) and once as the cap (R13-05, 'not worth buying a third time'); the cap is the same counter read the other way, so it is one rule, not two. R00-53 and V00-66 name a DIFFERENT 'second moving average gap bar setup' -- first gap bar, then a reversal toward the EMA that fails to reach it, then the next reversal -- which is this rule with PullbackDepthBeyondEma (depth 0, negated) supplying the failed-reach; both were graded hard and low confidence and are kept as citations rather than a second rule. Carried as a composite because it is a named book setup: it is EmaGapBarBreakoutEntry gated by leg_counting's SecondSignal (T21-28's price proxy -- a trigger fired and price traded back through the signal bar's extreme within N bars), and it should be authored on that machinery rather than a private counter.

xaverage_lag.description: The close last crossed the EMA at least N bars ago -- the trend is mature (Brooks: 30 or more bars).
xaverage_lag.pseudocode: barsSinceCrossUp = (close[0] > ema(close, emaLength)[0] && close[1] <= ema(close, emaLength)[1]) ? 0 : barsSinceCrossUp[1] + 1; barsSinceCrossUp >= minTrendBars

complexity.reason: an EMA plus a persistent bars-since-cross counter

xaverage_lag.merge_notes: TP3-30 offers two proxies for 'how old is this trend' -- bars since the close crossed the EMA, or the bar offset of the window's lowest low. The cross counter is chosen: it needs no Lowest window, it reuses CloseCrossesEma's test as its reset, and it degrades gracefully in a range (the counter simply stays small). Brooks's use is a warning, not a signal -- a trend past 30 bars often breaks out unusually strongly but may be an exhaustion climax -- so the placement's direction is the author's call. Distinct from EmaGapBarRun, which counts bars since the average was TOUCHED rather than since the close last crossed it.

blocked.description: This bar is a bull reversal bar and another bull reversal bar formed within the last N bars with at least one non-signal bar between them - take only the second attempt (mirror for bear).

complexity.reason: a window scan of a derived per-bar classification, so the classification must be evaluated at every offset in the window rather than at a fixed one

catalog_match.note: Structurally the same shape as TailBarCountDominance (a CountIF over a derived per-bar series), but the counted condition and the use are different.

blocked.merge_notes: Two volumes, one 'second entry' idea. Window 6 (V02-20) vs 10 (T10-03); default 10. V02-20 additionally requires the first signal to have FAILED (a later bar broke its low); T10-03's simpler 'the trend resumed for a bar or two' reading wins on mechanizability, and the strict failure test is the harder FailedReversalAttempt rule. Authoring note: the counted condition is a true series, so its offsets shift per counted bar, as in TailBarCountDominance.

blocked.description: Set the profit target just under the worst adverse excursion the trade has already survived, on the premise that the market usually rallies back at least as far as it first went against you.

complexity.reason: the mirror of the corpus's MaxPositionProfit peak tracker -- needs an equivalent trough accessor

blocked.merge_notes: Unusually precise for Brooks -- stated almost as a mechanical rule ('increase your profit target to one or two ticks less than the risk'). B rather than A only because MinPositionProfit is not yet in the register; it is the exact mirror of MaxPositionProfit, which ProfitProtector already uses, so the port is mechanical.

blocked.description: Block COUNTERTREND entries for blockBars bars after a spike: no run of spikeBars consecutive bull trend bars has completed within the last blockBars bars (mirror: no bear spike, blocking longs). Brooks: most traders who fade a spike lose, 'because most of the pullbacks do not fall far enough for a profit'.
blocked.pseudocode: barsSince(spikeBars consecutive bull trend bars completed) > blockBars

complexity.reason: a bars-since counter keyed on the consecutive-trend-bar detector

blocked.merge_notes: Single source. Same shape as PostClimaxCorrectionBlock but a different trigger event (a plain spike, bar_anatomy_trend_doji's ConsecutiveTrendBars, not a climax) and it blocks the OPPOSITE side, so it is not that rule with a parameter changed - the event detector lives inside the rule and the pane cannot substitute one for the other. Kept separate for that reason. TP3-41's page-310 note, 'after a strong breakout the bears might not look to sell again for dozens of bars', is the same test at a much larger blockBars and is why the input should be optimized rather than pinned at 10.
